For anyone else to do so was a sign of humility ([1 Sm 25:41](1Sam.25.41); [Lk 7:44-47](Luke.7.44-Luke.7.47); [Jn 13:3-16](John.13.3-John.13.16); [1 Tm 5:10](1Tim.5.10)).

Most biblical references to washing or bathing deal with ritual cleansing. Priests and Levites were required to wash their clothes and faces, and sometimes bodies, before approaching the altar and on ceremonial occasions ([Ex 29:4](Exod.29.4); [30:19-21](Exod.30.19-Exod.30.21); [40:7, 12, 30-32](Exod.40.7 Exod.40.12 Exod.40.30-Exod.40.32); [Nm 8:21](Num.8.21)). Before a slain animal was sacrificed, its legs and intestines were washed ([Lv 1:9, 13](Lev.1.9 Lev.1.13); [8:21](Lev.8.21); [9:14](Lev.9.14)). Anyone who was once unclean (e.g., a leper who was healed or someone who had experienced a genital discharge) had to wash his or her clothes and bathe to be ritually pure ([Lv 14:8-10](Lev.14.8-Lev.14.10); [15:5-11, 21-27](Lev.15.5-Lev.15.11 Lev.15.21-Lev.15.27)). Any garment that became polluted had to be ceremonially cleansed ([Lv 6:27](Lev.6.27); [13:54](Lev.13.54)).

“Washing” is also used figuratively for a cleansing from sin ([Ps 51:2](Ps.51.2); [Is 1:16](Isa.1.16); [4:4](Isa.4.4); [Jer 2:22](Jer.2.22); [4:14](Jer.4.14); [1 Cor 6:11](1Cor.6.11); [Heb 10:22](Heb.10.22)).
Gate in the city of Heshbon near which were several pools of clear water. A poetic biblical passage described a young woman’s eyes as being like those pools ([Sg 7:4](Song.7.4)).

Uriah’s wife, with whom David committed adultery and whom he later married. Bathsheba, also spelled Bathshua ([1 Chr 3:5](1Chr.3.5)), was the daughter of Ammiel or Eliam ([2 Sm 11:3](2Sam.11.3)) and possibly the granddaughter of Ahithophel, the king’s adviser ([2 Sm 15:12](2Sam.15.12); [23:34](2Sam.23.34)). Her Hittite husband was one of David’s top military heroes ([2 Sm 23:39](2Sam.23.39)).

While Uriah was off fighting under Joab, King David saw a beautiful woman taking her evening bath. Discovering her name and that her husband was away on duty, he sent for Bathsheba and had sexual intercourse with her ([2 Sm 11:1-4](2Sam.11.1-2Sam.11.4)). When Bathsheba later informed him that she was pregnant, the king ordered Uriah back to Jerusalem, hoping that the husband’s return would make Bathsheba’s pregnancy appear legitimate. But Uriah considered himself still on active duty and slept with the palace guard, refusing to go home (vv [5-13](2Sam.11.5-2Sam.11.13)). Frustrated, David sent him back to the front and ordered Joab to put Uriah in the front lines and then pull back. Consequently, Uriah was killed (vv [14-25](2Sam.11.14-2Sam.11.25)).

After Bathsheba’s period of mourning, David installed her in the palace as his seventh wife, and she bore the child. The Lord sent the prophet Nathan to pronounce judgment on David’s sin through a parable. Nathan prophesied a series of tragedies in David’s household, beginning with the death of Bathsheba’s infant son ([2 Sm 11:26–12:14](2Sam.11.26-2Sam.12.14)). David confessed his sin and repented, but the infant became sick and died. The prologue (or superscription) of [Psalm 51](Ps.51.1-Ps.51.19) describes it as the psalm of repentance David wrote when confronted by Nathan over his adultery with Bathsheba and his murder of Uriah. David comforted Bathsheba, and eventually they had other children ([2 Sm 12:15-25](2Sam.12.15-2Sam.12.25)).

Of David’s 19 sons by his seven wives ([1 Chr 3:1-9](1Chr.3.1-1Chr.3.9)), the sons born to Bathsheba were Shimea (also spelled Shammua, [2 Sm 5:14](2Sam.5.14); [1 Chr 14:4](1Chr.14.4)), Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. Nathan ([Lk 3:31](Luke.3.31)) and Solomon ([Mt 1:6](Matt.1.6)) appear in NT genealogies of Jesus Christ. Bathsheba also appears in Matthew’s genealogy under the description “she who had been the wife of Uriah.” At the very end of David’s life, the prophet Nathan told Bathsheba that David’s son Adonijah (by his wife Haggith) was conspiring to usurp the throne. Bathsheba and Nathan persuaded David to make Solomon king as he had promised ([1 Kgs 1](1Kgs.1.1-1Kgs.1.53)).
*See also* [David](dictionary:David).
1. Canaanite wife of Judah who bore him three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah ([Gn 38:2-5](Gen.38.2-Gen.38.5); [1 Chr 2:3](1Chr.2.3)).
2. Alternate spelling of Bathsheba in [1 Chronicles 3:5](1Chr.3.5). *See* [Bathsheba](dictionary:Bathsheba).

Ancient military machine with a heavy wooden beam used to batter down gates or walls. Some battering rams had an iron ram’s head at the end of the beam. *See* [Armor and Weapons](dictionary:ArmorandWeapons).
Heavy ax with a wide blade used as a weapon of war. *See* [Armor and Weapons](dictionary:ArmorandWeapons).

Defensive wall, with openings for shooting, on top of a fortress; by extension, a parapet or railing around any flat roof. Houses in the Near East were built with flat roofs, which were used for many different purposes. Rahab hid two Israelite spies on her roof ([Jos 2:6](Josh.2.6)). Saul slept on Samuel’s roof ([1 Sm 9:25](1Sam.9.25)). King David from his roof saw Bathsheba taking a bath ([2 Sm 11:2](2Sam.11.2)). People celebrated on rooftops ([Is 22:1-2](Isa.22.1-Isa.22.2)). Peter prayed on his roof ([Acts 10:9](Acts.10.9)). With so much activity on rooftops, it is easy to understand the need for the law “When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house, if any one fall from it” ([Dt 22:8](Deut.22.8), RSV).

City walls often had battlements at the gates and corners from which the city could be defended from attack. Hebrew words for such fortifications are often translated “towers” ([2 Chr 26:15](2Chr.26.15); [Zep 1:16](Zeph.1.16)).

Individual who directed the repair of a section of the Jerusalem wall under Nehemiah’s supervision ([Neh 3:18](Neh.3.18)). Bavvai was Henadad’s son and the official of half the district of Keilah, a town 17 miles (27.4 kilometers) southwest of Jerusalem. Binnui ([Neh 3:24](Neh.3.24)), also mentioned as Henadad’s son (cf. [Ezr 3:9](Ezra.3.9)), may be a corrupted spelling of Bavvai, or the two may have been brothers. *See* [Binnui #4](dictionary:Binnui).
Tree 40 to 60 feet (12 to 18 meters) high with fragrant, evergreen leaves and native to the Holy Land. *See* [Plants (Laurel or Sweet Bay)](dictionary:Plants).
Ancestor of a group of temple assistants returning to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Ezr 2:52](Ezra.2.52), “Bazluth”; [Neh 7:54](Neh.7.54)).

Substance mentioned twice in the OT, evidently the resinous gum of an Arabian shrub (known scientifically as *Commiphora africana*). The same genus of Middle Eastern plants includes the shrub from which myrrh is derived and possibly the one from which the biblical “balm” was obtained.

Apart from the Bible, bdellium was described by an English herbalist as an aromatic gum from a tree known in Persia and eastward. In the first century AD the Roman writer Pliny mentioned the same tree and described the gum as waxlike and looking like pearl.

The manna gathered by the Israelites is described in the Bible as having the same color as bdellium ([Nm 11:7](Num.11.7)). Bdellium is also mentioned along with the gold and onyx stone found near the Garden of Eden ([Gn 2:12](Gen.2.12)). Because it was included in that list, bdellium was once thought to be pearl or a precious stone.
*See also* [Plants](dictionary:Plants).
Warrior from Benjamin’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul. Bealiah was one of David’s ambidextrous archers and slingers ([1 Chr 12:5](1Chr.12.5)).
1. Town along the border of Edom in the Negev Desert area ([Jos 15:24](Josh.15.24)).
2. Administrative district in the time of King Solomon governed by Baana, Hushai’s son ([1 Kgs 4:16](1Kgs.4.16)).

1. Weaver’s beam—round wooden roller on which the cloth or carpet was wound during the weaving process in Bible times. The spears of the giant Goliath ([1 Sm 17:7](1Sam.17.7); [2 Sm 21:19](2Sam.21.19); [1 Chr 20:5](1Chr.20.5)) and an Egyptian killed by Benaiah, one of David’s mighty men ([1 Chr 11:23](1Chr.11.23)), were compared to a weaver’s beam.

2. Tree trunk or log that has been squared and used for building purposes. King Solomon used beams and planks of cedar to build the temple ([1 Kgs 6:9](1Kgs.6.9); [2 Chr 3:7](2Chr.3.7)) and his “House of the Forest of Lebanon” ([1 Kgs 7:2, 12](1Kgs.7.2 1Kgs.7.12)). Another mention of cedar beams probably refers to their aroma ([Sg 1:17](Song.1.17)).
3. Crossbeam of a Hebrew balance from which the scales were hung by cords.

4. Beam (KJV) or log (RSV) referred to by Jesus ([Mt 7:3-5](Matt.7.3-Matt.7.5); [Lk 6:41-42](Luke.6.41-Luke.6.42)). Jesus contrasted the beam in an accuser’s eye with the mote (KJV) or speck (RSV) in his brother’s eye.

Any of various plants of the legume family, and part of the diet of the peoples of Bible lands. *See* [Agriculture](dictionary:Agriculture); [Plants](dictionary:Plants); [Food and Food Preparation](dictionary:FoodandFoodPreparation).

Large, short-tailed, shaggy animal that feeds on plants as well as small animals. The bear mentioned several times in the Bible is the Syrian brown bear still found in Syria and Turkey but no longer in Israel. *See* [Animals](dictionary:Animals).
Constellation of stars (Ursa Major, also known as the Big Dipper) mentioned in [Job 9:9](Job.9.9) and [38:32](Job.38.32). *See* [Astronomy](dictionary:Astronomy).

Hair growing on the lower part of a man’s face, worn as a sign of maturity among all ancient Semitic peoples, including the Israelites. Among the Israelites, care of the beard took on religious significance ([Lv 19:27](Lev.19.27)). Levitical law prohibited priests from shaving their heads or clipping their beards ([21:5-6](Lev.21.5-Lev.21.6)). David’s ambassadors to an Ammonite king were humiliated by having one side of their beards shaved off by the Ammonites. That indignity and others led to war ([2 Sm 10:1-8](2Sam.10.1-2Sam.10.8)). Removal of an Israelite’s beard, however, was considered appropriate under certain circumstances. Suspicion of leprosy on the head or face required shaving around the suspected spot to permit better diagnosis ([Lv 13:29-37](Lev.13.29-Lev.13.37)). A shaven head, along with wailing and the wearing of sackcloth, was a way of proclaiming impending or prevailing doom ([Is 15:1-3](Isa.15.1-Isa.15.3)). Ezra dramatized Israel’s spiritual disaster by pulling hair out of his head and beard ([Ezr 9:3](Ezra.9.3)).

Animal in both the OT and NT, having in some cases a figurative significance. The word has a variety of meanings in the OT. Some of the diversity is due to inconsistent translations of several Hebrew words that can signify “living creature” as well as “beast,” but which have sometimes been translated only as “beast.” In the OT, therefore, beast can refer to the following:

1. In general, any animal (e.g., [Gn 1:24](Gen.1.24); [Ps 36:6](Ps.36.6)), but often distinguished from fish, birds, and insects (e.g., [Gn 6:7](Gen.6.7); [Lv 11:2](Lev.11.2); [Dt 4:17](Deut.4.17); [Jb 12:7](Job.12.7); [35:11](Job.35.11); [Zep 1:3](Zeph.1.3)).
3. A wild and sometimes carnivorous animal (e.g., [Gn 37:20](Gen.37.20); [Ex 23:11](Exod.23.11); [Dt 28:26](Deut.28.26); [1 Sm 17:44](1Sam.17.44); [Ez 14:15](Ezek.14.15)).

4. The figurative usage of the word “beast” is most apparent in the books of Daniel and Revelation. In Daniel (especially [Dn 7](Dan.7.1-Dan.7.28)) the beast is a symbol of a world ruler who persecutes and oppresses the people of God. In Revelation the apostle John took over that concept with its vivid imagery to speak of the final persecution of God’s people at the end of history. John’s beast in its apostasy closely resembles the “antichrist” of his earlier epistles ([1 Jn 2:18, 22](1John.2.18 1John.2.22); [4:3](1John.4.3); [2 Jn 1:7](2John.1.7)) and Paul’s “man of lawlessness” ([2 Thes 2:3](2Thess.2.3)). Many Bible commentators regard the three as designating the same individual. *See* [Antichrist](dictionary:Antichrist); [Armageddon](dictionary:Armageddon); [Mark of the Beast](dictionary:MarkofGodMarkoftheBeast); [Revelation, Book of](dictionary:RevelationBookof).

Term derived from Latin *beatitudo;* it is not used in the English Bible. Technically it means “blessedness” as described in the OT and NT. “Blessed” is translated from both Hebrew and Greek words to refer to divine favor conveyed to people.

The formal utterance “happy is,” or “blessed is,” is a common declaration in the book of Psalms (used 26 times) and Proverbs (8 times). It is used 10 times in the other books of the OT and 13 times in the apocryphal books. These beatitudes are pronounced upon the person who is righteous, having faith and hope in God. They are signs of a life lived in proximity to Yahweh, in the experience of forgiveness, and in the love and favor of God. Such life is a totality, so such blessings are expressive of holistic enrichment, harmony, and fecundity, whether in family life, in temple worship, in public life, or in the interior of one’s own being. The person so blessed is in touch with the fruitfulness of the Creator himself. Such a one lives a fulfilled life, life as God intended it to be lived before him.

c.x: One day as he saw the crowds gathering, Jesus went up on the mountainside and sat down. His disciples gathered around him, **2** and he began to teach them.
**3** “God blesses those who are poor and realize their need for him,
for the Kingdom of Heaven is theirs.
**4** God blesses those who mourn,
for they will be comforted.
**5** God blesses those who are humble,
for they will inherit the whole earth.
**6** God blesses those who hunger and thirst for justice,
for they will be satisfied.
**7** God blesses those who are merciful,
for they will be shown mercy.
**8** God blesses those whose hearts are pure,
for they will see God.
**9** God blesses those who work for peace,
for they will be called the children of God.
**10** God blesses those who are persecuted for doing right,
for the Kingdom of Heaven is theirs.

**11** “God blesses you when people mock you and persecute you and lie about you and say all sorts of evil things against you because you are my followers. **12** Be happy about it! Be very glad! For a great reward awaits you in heaven. And remember, the ancient prophets were persecuted in the same way.

b.x: In the NT, references to “blessing” occur seven times in the book of Revelation, three times in the Epistle to the Romans, and once in John’s Gospel. The prominence of “blessedness” in Matthew and Luke gives rise to the technical term “Beatitudes.” There are interesting contrasts between Luke’s “sermon on the plain” ([Lk 6:20-23](Luke.6.20-Luke.6.23)) and Matthew’s “sermon on the mount” ([Mt 5:3-12](Matt.5.3-Matt.5.12)). The pronouncement of the blessings in Luke is done immediately after the selection of the 12 disciples ([Lk 6:12-16](Luke.6.12-Luke.6.16)). Yet the sermon is addressed to the crowd generally and speaks of the advent of God’s kingdom as the reversal of the social conditions of the human race. So Luke balances four blessings with four woes—changing from the present tense to the future tense—to heighten the contrast of the impending reversal of social conditions.

In Matthew’s account, the advent of the kingdom has already commenced, indicated by the use of the present tense. It is addressed to the disciples particularly and is not a general proclamation. The sermon is set within two statements of Jesus: he has not come to destroy but to fulfill the Mosaic law ([Mt 5:17](Matt.5.17)); and it is necessary to have a kind of righteousness that exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees ([Mt 5:20](Matt.5.20)). So these Beatitudes are more concerned with the interior life of the disciple, to activate here and now the kind of life Jesus communicates in those who follow him, for Jesus has already inaugurated the kingdom. These eight Beatitudes reflect on the traits of those who belong to that kingdom and who therefore reflect Christ’s own life. The people and situations described may seem pitiable by human standards, but because of God’s presence in their lives, they are actually blessed and should be congratulated and imitated. *See* [Jesus Christ, Life and Teachings of](dictionary:JesusChristTeachingsof).

Gate of Herod’s temple in Jerusalem where a man born lame was miraculously healed through the ministry of Peter and John ([Acts 3:2, 10](Acts.3.2 Acts.3.10)). The location of this gate is uncertain, but it was probably the gate leading from the Court of the Gentiles into the Women’s Court, called the Corinthian Gate (for its Corinthian bronze) by the Jewish historian Josephus. According to him, it measured 75 feet (22.9 meters) high by 60 feet (18.3 meters) wide. A burial inscription found on Mt Olivet attributes the building of the gate to an Alexandrian Jew named Nicanor.
*See also* [Temple](dictionary:Temple).

Harmonious combination of qualities pleasant to see. Archaeological materials indicate that the ancient Hebrews were concerned more with usefulness than with beauty. Hebrew pottery, for example, was generally more bulky than Canaanite pottery. Yet such artifacts do not mean that the Hebrews had no aesthetic appreciation.

The OT speaks of God’s creation as beautiful ([Gn 2:9](Gen.2.9); [Jb 26:13](Job.26.13); [Ps 19:1-6](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.6); [Sg 6:10](Song.6.10)). The land of Canaan is a “pleasant land” ([Jer 3:19](Jer.3.19)). Jerusalem is called “beautiful” ([Is 52:1](Isa.52.1); [Lam 2:15](Lam.2.15)), as is one of its temple gates ([Acts 3:2, 10](Acts.3.2 Acts.3.10)). The Hebrews admired the wild grandeur of the Lebanon mountain range ([Ps 104:16](Ps.104.16); [Is 60:13](Isa.60.13)). The Canaanite city of Tirzah (“beauty”), King Baasha’s capital in the northern kingdom ([1 Kgs 15:33](1Kgs.15.33)), was so named for its attractive location.

Although the Hebrews did not exalt the human form as did the ancient Greeks, the OT does idealize physical attractiveness. A bride’s beauty is described eloquently by her bridegroom in love lyrics in [Song of Songs 4:1-15](Song.4.1-Song.4.15); [6:4](Song.6.4). Such praise of the bride may have been a traditional feature of Israelite weddings. Several women prominent in the OT are described as beautiful ([Gn 29:17](Gen.29.17); [2 Sm 11:2](2Sam.11.2); [Est 2:7](Esth.2.7)). But sensual beauty was secondary to industry, resourcefulness, and traditional piety in a woman ([Prv 31:10-31](Prov.31.10-Prov.31.31)). A number of men also were known for their physical attractiveness—for example, David ([1 Sm 16:12](1Sam.16.12)) and Absalom ([2 Sm 14:25](2Sam.14.25)). Cosmetics, jewelry, and other accessories were used as female beauty aids in OT times. The prophet Isaiah listed such items ([Is 3:18-24](Isa.3.18-Isa.3.24)), and Ezekiel mentioned cosmetic practices current in his day ([Ez 16:10-13](Ezek.16.10-Ezek.16.13)). Israelite worship was beautiful, too, with the high priest’s elaborate ceremonial robes designed for glory and beauty ([Ex 28:2, 40](Exod.28.2 Exod.28.40)).

The concept of beauty is applied also to God in the OT. The Lord’s favor is called his “beauty” ([Ps 90:17](Ps.90.17)). Isaiah recorded God’s promise to give his people “beauty for ashes” ([Is 61:3](Isa.61.3)). The psalmist expressed a desire to spend time in the temple enjoying the Lord’s beauty, his “incomparable perfections” ([Ps 27:4](Ps.27.4)). Isaiah described God as a “diadem of beauty” to the faithful Israelite remnant ([Is 28:5](Isa.28.5)), and the Messiah was spoken of as a beautiful king ([33:17](Isa.33.17)). Thus in the OT the concept of beauty had a deeper meaning than simply physical attractiveness. It became a theological concept affirming God’s essential glory.

The NT urges Christ’s followers to live lives that will “adorn” the teaching of the Savior, making it attractive to nonbelievers ([Ti 2:10](Titus.2.10)). Those who preach the gospel of Christ are spoken of as beautiful ([Rom 10:15](Rom.10.15)). The apostles Paul and Peter warned women against being satisfied with outward beauty ([1 Tm 2:9-10](1Tim.2.9-1Tim.2.10)), reminding them that beautiful character is the true adornment of godliness ([1 Pt 3:3-5](1Pet.3.3-1Pet.3.5)). The beauty of the believer’s final home in heaven is reflected in the description of the “new Jerusalem” as a bride and in the symbolism of treasured precious stones of antiquity (see [Rv 21–22](Rev.21.1-Rev.22.21)).

1. Ancestor of a family that returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Ezr 2:11](Ezra.2.11); [8:11](Ezra.8.11); [Neh 7:16](Neh.7.16)). Some of the members of that family were guilty of marrying foreign women ([Ezr 10:28](Ezra.10.28)).

2. Levitical leader of Israel who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile ([Neh 10:15](Neh.10.15)). This individual was perhaps a member of the family of #1 above.
Unidentified Israelite city mentioned in Judith 15:4.
1. Benjamin’s second son, who migrated to Egypt with his grandfather Jacob ([Gn 46:21](Gen.46.21); [1 Chr 7:6](1Chr.7.6)).
2. Ephraim’s second son, from whom the family of Becherites originated ([Nm 26:35](Num.26.35)). He is also called Bered ([1 Chr 7:20](1Chr.7.20)).
Zeror’s father, a member of Benjamin’s tribe and an ancestor of King Saul ([1 Sm 9:1](1Sam.9.1)).
Plain mentioned only in the Apocrypha. Nebuchadnezzar’s general, Holofernes, camped there on his western conquest (Jdt 2:21-23).
*See* [Furniture](dictionary:Furniture).
Father of Hadad, one of the kings of Edom before the Israelite monarchy ([Gn 36:35](Gen.36.35); [1 Chr 1:46](1Chr.1.46)).

1. One of Israel’s deliverers, along with Gideon, Jephthah, and Samuel, during the time of the judges ([1 Sm 12:11](1Sam.12.11), KJV; RSV mg). The name Bedan may be either a shortened form of Abdon ([Jgs 12:13](Judg.12.13)) or a scribal error for Barak ([Jgs 4:6](Judg.4.6)).
2. Ulam’s son, a descendant of Manasseh ([1 Chr 7:17](1Chr.7.17)).
Bani’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile ([Ezr 10:35](Ezra.10.35)).
*See* [Animals](dictionary:Animals).
Former name of Eliada, one of King David’s sons, in [1 Chronicles 14:7](1Chr.14.7). *See* [Eliada #1](dictionary:Eliada).

Epithet meaning “lord of the flies” or “lord of the manure pile,” referring to Satan. It was used against Jesus by his enemies ([Mt 10:25](Matt.10.25), KJV “Beelzebub”; [12:24](Matt.12.24); [Lk 11:15](Luke.11.15)). *See* [Baal-zebub](dictionary:BaalZebub).

1. Israelite campsite on their wilderness journey, probably just north of the Arnon River on the Moabite-Amorite border ([Nm 21:16](Num.21.16)). The name means “a well.” Water from the well they dug there was commemorated in a song ([Nm 21:17-18](Num.21.17-Num.21.18)). A Moabite well that was later called Beer-elim ([Is 15:8](Isa.15.8)) may have been the same location. *See* [Wilderness Wanderings](dictionary:WildernessWanderings).

2. Place to which Gideon’s son Jotham escaped after telling a parable against his half brother Abimelech, who had killed all the other sons of Gideon in an attempt to become king of Israel ([Jgs 9:21](Judg.9.21)).
Zophah’s son, a warrior in Asher’s tribe ([1 Chr 7:37](1Chr.7.37)).
Chief of Reuben’s tribe ([1 Chr 5:6, 26](1Chr.5.6 1Chr.5.26)) taken captive by the Assyrian king Tilgath-pilneser (a later spelling of Tiglath-pileser).
One of the cities of Moab that Isaiah predicted would hear wailing at the fall of the Moabite kingdom ([Is 15:8](Isa.15.8)); perhaps the same as Beer ([Nm 21:16](Num.21.16)).
1. Judith’s Hittite (Hethite) father. Judith was one of the wives of Esau ([Gn 26:34](Gen.26.34)).
2. Father of Hosea the prophet ([Hos 1:1](Hos.1.1)).

Well between Kadesh and Bered where Hagar, pregnant with Ishmael, was confronted by the angel of the Lord ([Gn 16:7-14](Gen.16.7-Gen.16.14)). The name given to the site means “the well of the Living One who sees me,” referring to God’s appearance to Sarai’s servant girl. Later, it became a frequent watering place for Isaac on his travels ([Gn 24:62](Gen.24.62); [25:11](Gen.25.11)).

One of four Hivite cities that secured Joshua’s promise not to destroy them when the Israelites marched into Canaan ([Jos 9:17](Josh.9.17)). Beeroth was later identified as a city in Benjamin’s territory ([Jos 18:25](Josh.18.25); [2 Sm 4:2-3](2Sam.4.2-2Sam.4.3)). It was the home of Rechab and Baanah, assassins of King Ishbosheth ([2 Sm 4:2-9](2Sam.4.2-2Sam.4.9)), and of Naharai, Joab’s armor bearer ([2 Sm 23:37](2Sam.23.37); [1 Chr 11:39](1Chr.11.39)). The city was repopulated after the exile ([Ezr 2:25](Ezra.2.25); [Neh 7:29](Neh.7.29)). El Bireh near Ramallah and Nebi Samwil north of Jerusalem have both been suggested as possible locations for Beeroth.

Site where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey from Egypt, near Moserah or Moseroth ([Dt 10:6](Deut.10.6); see NLT mg); also called Bene-jaakan in [Numbers 33:31-32](Num.33.31-Num.33.32). Beeroth Bene-jaakan means “well of Jaakan’s sons.” *See* [Wilderness Wanderings](dictionary:WildernessWanderings).
Inhabitant of Beeroth ([2 Sm 4:2-9](2Sam.4.2-2Sam.4.9), KJV, RSV). *See* [Beeroth](dictionary:Beeroth).

Scriptural designation for the southern extremity of the Promised Land, located 28 miles (45.1 kilometers) southwest of Hebron. It was an important Negev site at an early time. Hagar wandered with Ishmael in this area, as did Abraham. Later Isaac ([Gn 26:23](Gen.26.23)) and Jacob ([46:1](Gen.46.1)) both had significant spiritual experiences there, and later yet it was important in the lives of numerous other Hebrews.

Beersheba of the Hebrew monarchy period was located at Tell Beersheba, two miles (3.2 kilometers) northeast of the modern city. Recent excavations reveal that the city was founded by the Hebrews in the 12th or 11th century BC and probably was the place where the sons of Samuel judged the people ([1 Sm 8:2](1Sam.8.2)).

This city was only about two and a half acres (one hectare) in size. In its ruins there were the remains of a horned altar, which when reassembled stood to a height of about five feet (1.5 meters). This is the same height as the altar found at Arad, and the two are the only Hebrew altars yet found that date to the period of the first temple. These altars were the same height as the one in the tabernacle ([Ex 27:1](Exod.27.1)) and probably the same as the original altar in Solomon’s temple ([2 Chr 6:13](2Chr.6.13)). A great water system was also uncovered similar to those of Megiddo and Hazor.

City of the half-tribe of Manasseh given to the Levitical family of Gershonites in the partitioning of the Promised Land ([Jos 21:27](Josh.21.27)). The spelling is a shortened form for Beth-ashtaroth (“house or place of Ashtaroth”). It seems to be the same as the city of Ashtaroth found in a similar passage ([1 Chr 6:71](1Chr.6.71)). *See* [Ashtaroth, Ashterathite](dictionary:AshtarothAshterathite); [Levitical Cities](dictionary:LeviticalCities).
KJV for cricket in [Leviticus 11:22](Lev.11.22). *See* [Animals (Cricket)](dictionary:Animals).
One who asks for charity, especially one who lives by begging, a mendicant.

Biblical references to begging are limited to such Hebrew verbs as “to seek” or “to ask,” and, as a noun, to “the poor and needy”; in the NT, Greek terms refer to being “poor” or “miserable,” and to those who “ask for more.” Professional beggars were unknown in Moses’ time, since the law made ample provision for taking care of the poor.

Earliest legislation ([Dt 15:11](Deut.15.11)) mandated the care of those who were poor. There were regulations such as the Sabbath year, the year of remission to those indebted ([Lv 25](Lev.25.1-Lev.25.55)). In that year the produce of the land was left to the poor and destitute ([Ex 23:11](Exod.23.11)), and all debts were canceled ([Dt 15:1](Deut.15.1)). The duty of lending liberally to the poor was promoted (vv [7-11](Deut.15.7-Deut.15.11)), and hired laborers were protected ([24:14-15](Deut.24.14-Deut.24.15)). The purpose was that “there should be no more poor among you” ([15:4](Deut.15.4)). Indeed, in the early days of Israelite settlement, all Israelites enjoyed a comparable standard of living.

In excavations at Tirsah near Nablus, the size and arrangements of houses of the tenth century BC are all about the same. By the eighth century BC, there is a striking contrast, with houses on the same site clearly divided into the town’s richer and poorer quarters. The social revolution between those two centuries was associated with the rise of the Israelite monarchy and growth of a class of officials who gained private profits from their positions. The prophets condemned the fact that wealth was ill-gotten and badly distributed in their day (e.g., [Is 5:8](Isa.5.8); [Hos 12:8](Hos.12.8); [Am 8:4-7](Amos.8.4-Amos.8.7); [Mi 2:2](Mic.2.2)). The prophet Amos denounced creditors who felt no pity for the poor ([Am 2:6-8](Amos.2.6-Amos.2.8); [8:6](Amos.8.6)). Yet, throughout the OT, there is essentially no reference to beggars. During the intertestamental period, however, almsgiving became an important religious duty.

In the NT, begging seems to be prevalent. In the ministry of Jesus, references are made to a blind beggar ([Jn 9:8-9](John.9.8-John.9.9)), to blind Bartimaeus ([Mk 10:46-52](Mark.10.46-Mark.10.52)), and to Lazarus, a godly beggar who is contrasted with a rich man ([Lk 16:19-31](Luke.16.19-Luke.16.31)). The apostles Peter and John encountered a crippled beggar by the “Beautiful,” or Nicanor, Gate in Jerusalem ([Acts 3:1-11](Acts.3.1-Acts.3.11)). Jesus rebuked an ostentatious show of almsgiving ([Mt 6:1-4](Matt.6.1-Matt.6.4)) but stressed the importance of giving to the poor from right motives ([Mt 5:42-48](Matt.5.42-Matt.5.48)). By the time of Jesus, Jerusalem had become a center for beggars, probably because almsgiving in the Holy City was then regarded as particularly meritorious. Begging in Jerusalem was concentrated around the holy places. The pool of Beth-zatha was a place of healing, and the sick, blind, lame, and paralyzed lay there to beg as well as to get into the waters for healing ([Jn 5:2-9](John.5.2-John.5.9)).

In the early Christian community, the first organization of officers was made to provide for a fair distribution of funds to the poor ([Acts 4:32-35](Acts.4.32-Acts.4.35); [6:1-6](Acts.6.1-Acts.6.6)). On the first day of each week, some portion of each Christian’s income was to be allotted to the needy ([11:27-30](Acts.11.27-Acts.11.30); [Rom 15:25-27](Rom.15.25-Rom.15.27); [1 Cor 16:1-4](1Cor.16.1-1Cor.16.4)). Possibly the poverty of Palestine was made worse by heavy Roman taxation; tax gatherers as well as beggars are prominent in the Gospel narratives. It has also been suggested that the rise of the Zealots was closely associated with the social factor of poverty; the revolutionary Zealots were largely comprised of society’s “dregs,” according to the Jewish historian Josephus. In AD 66 the Zealots burned the Jerusalem archives, no doubt intending to destroy the records of their debts kept there. Josephus reports that before the Roman destruction of Jerusalem, gangs of beggars were terrorizing the whole city. *See* [Alms](dictionary:Alms); [Poor, The](dictionary:Poorthe).
Form of execution practiced in Bible times. *See* [Criminal Law and Punishment](dictionary:CriminalLawandPunishment).

Hebrew word in plural form usually translated “beasts” or “wild animals” (as in [Dt 28:26](Deut.28.26); [32:24](Deut.32.24); [Ps 50:10](Ps.50.10); [Is 18:6](Isa.18.6); 2 Esd 6:49, 51; [Hb 2:17](Hab.2.17)). Most English versions refer only once to “behemoth,” where the context seems to refer to a specific animal, large and powerful, believed by many biblical scholars to be the hippopotamus ([Jb 40:15](Job.40.15)). In ancient times, the hippopotamus was well known in Egypt and may have inhabited the Jordan Valley. [Job 40:23](Job.40.23) may, however, refer to any river swollen like the Jordan in flood season.
*See* [Animals](dictionary:Animals).
*See* [Inscriptions](dictionary:Inscriptions).
Six-gram weight called “half a shekel, by the shekel of the sanctuary” ([Ex 38:26](Exod.38.26)). *See* [Weights and Measures](dictionary:WeightsandMeasures).
Alternate spelling for Ephraim’s second son ([Nm 26:35](Num.26.35)) and his descendants. *See* [Becher, Becherite #2](dictionary:BecherBecherite).

Title of the state god of Babylon, Marduk, mentioned disdainfully by Isaiah ([Is 46:1](Isa.46.1)). Jeremiah speaks of Bel ([Jer 50:2](Jer.50.2); [51:44](Jer.51.44)), and Bel is the idol in the apocryphal Bel and the Dragon. *See* [Marduk](dictionary:Marduk).

1. Beor’s son, a king of Edom who ruled before Israel had a king ([Gn 36:31-33](Gen.36.31-Gen.36.33)). Because Balaam, the pagan prophet from north Syria, also had a father named Beor ([Nm 22:5](Num.22.5)), some ancients and a number of modern critical scholars have confused the Edomite Bela with Balaam.
2. Benjamin’s oldest son ([Gn 46:21](Gen.46.21); [1 Chr 8:1](1Chr.8.1)), whose descendants were called Belaites ([Nm 26:38](Num.26.38)).

3. Azaz’s son, a descendant of Reuben who lived in Gilead in Transjordan. So vast were his family’s holdings that they pastured their cattle as far east as the Euphrates River ([1 Chr 5:8-9](1Chr.5.8-1Chr.5.9)). In the reign of Saul, his family successfully held their land against Hagrite opposition.
Alternate name for Zoar, a city of the plain, in [Genesis 14:2](Gen.14.2). *See* [Cities of the Plain](dictionary:CitiesofthePlain); [Zoar](dictionary:Zoar).

KJV rendering of Bela, Benjamin’s oldest son, in [1 Chronicles 8:1](1Chr.8.1). His descendants were called Belaites ([Nm 26:38-40](Num.26.38-Num.26.40); see NLT). *See* [Bela (Person) #2](dictionary:BelaPerson).
*See* [Daniel, Additions to](dictionary:DanielAdditionsto).

Common Hebrew noun meaning “baseness,” “worthlessness,” “wickedness,” or “lawlessness.” Belial, however, is often rendered as a proper noun. Thus, such translations as “sons of Belial” appear ([Jgs 19:22](Judg.19.22); [1 Sm 2:12](1Sam.2.12), KJV), “daughter of Belial” ([1 Sm 1:16](1Sam.1.16)), or “children of Belial” ([Dt 13:13](Deut.13.13); [Jgs 20:13](Judg.20.13)). Newer translations generally prefer the common noun form and give such readings as “worthless rabble” or simply “worthless” and the like ([Dt 13:13](Deut.13.13); [Jgs 19:22](Judg.19.22); [20:13](Judg.20.13); [1 Sm 1:16](1Sam.1.16); [2:12](1Sam.2.12); [10:27](1Sam.10.27); [Prv 6:12](Prov.6.12)). One possible exception to this rule is found in [Nahum 1:15](Nah.1.15), which some scholars think should be rendered as “Belial,” a personalized designation of the Assyrian conqueror who had been a threat to the southern kingdom of Judah.

Intertestamental literature often used “Belial” as a proper noun and thus prepared the way for its NT usage. In the NT the term appears once as “Belial” (or Beliar in [2 Cor 6:15](2Cor.6.15)) and is identified with Satan, the personification of all that is evil. Noncanonical writings of the NT period commonly used it as a name for Satan or the Antichrist.

Conviction based on testimony that something is true or that someone is reliable. As used in the Bible, to believe in God involves the element of trust, not mere acknowledgment of his existence. *See* [Faith](dictionary:Faith).

Those who believe; in the NT, specifically, those who believe in Jesus as Lord and follow him ([Acts 5:14](Acts.5.14)). One would expect the term “believers” (sometimes translated “faithful”) to be a title for Christians, since the NT stresses belief in Jesus. Although NT authors emphasized believing, they rarely used the term “believer” as a name for Christians. There are a few clear examples ([Acts 4:32](Acts.4.32); [10:45](Acts.10.45); [19:18](Acts.19.18); [1 Tm 4:12](1Tim.4.12)), but in other places the term is a description, not a name ([Acts 2:44](Acts.2.44); [15:5](Acts.15.5); [18:27](Acts.18.27); [1 Tm 4:3](1Tim.4.3)). As a name, “believer” points to the personal commitment of Christians to Jesus. Christians were called not merely to believe something but to give themselves to someone.

Small noisemaker. Bells were intermittently attached between ornamental pomegranates around the lower hem of the high priestly robe ([Ex 28:33-34](Exod.28.33-Exod.28.34); [39:25-26](Exod.39.25-Exod.39.26)). *See* [Musical Instruments (Pamonim)](dictionary:MusicalInstruments); [Music](dictionary:Music).
Samaritan city that served as a camp for Nebuchadnezzar’s invading general, Holofernes, against the Jews (Jdt 4:1-4). Probably the same as Balbaim (7:3), Balamon (8:3), and perhaps Bebai (15:4).

Designation of one disciple, evidently the author of the Gospel of John ([Jn 21:20-24](John.21.20-John.21.24)). Five passages in John’s Gospel mention the disciple whom Jesus loved: (1) The disciple whom Jesus loved lay close to Jesus’ chest during the Last Supper and was beckoned by Peter to ask Jesus who the betrayer would be ([13:21-26](John.13.21-John.13.26)). (2) The disciple whom Jesus loved stood near the cross, and Mary the mother of Jesus was given to his care ([19:25-27](John.19.25-John.19.27)). (3) Mary Magdalene came to Peter and the disciple whom Jesus loved, reporting that Jesus’ body was missing from the tomb ([20:2](John.20.2)). (4) The disciple whom Jesus loved was in a fishing boat with Peter and the other disciples and recognized Jesus standing on the shore ([21:7](John.21.7)). (5) The disciple whom Jesus loved was following Jesus by the lakeshore, and the author reminded his readers that this was the same disciple spoken of at the Last Supper ([21:20-23](John.21.20-John.21.23); cf. [13:21-26](John.13.21-John.13.26)).
Because the phrase is found only in John’s Gospel, could it be the author’s way of referring to himself? Several passages make that seem very likely.

A list of names given in [John 21:2](John.21.2) indicates that the disciples present at the lakeshore were Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee (James and John), and two others. Evidently the beloved disciple was one of the sons of Zebedee or else one of the two unnamed disciples.

The beloved disciple was almost certainly one of the Twelve, since he was present at the Last Supper, and evidently only the 12 disciples were there with Jesus ([Mt 26:20](Matt.26.20); [Mk 14:17-20](Mark.14.17-Mark.14.20); [Lk 22:14, 30](Luke.22.14 Luke.22.30)). That eliminates Lazarus and John Mark, who have sometimes been suggested as possibilities for the beloved disciple.

The beloved disciple appeared to be close to Peter ([Jn 13:23-24](John.13.23-John.13.24); [20:2](John.20.2); [21:7](John.21.7); see also [Acts 3](Acts.3.1-Acts.3.26); [8:14](Acts.8.14); [Gal 2:9](Gal.2.9)). Matthew, Mark, and Luke record that Peter, James, and John were constantly selected by Jesus to be with him. Since Peter was mentioned in connection with the disciple whom Jesus loved, and since James was martyred early ([Acts 12:2](Acts.12.2)), only John is left as a reasonable possibility—if, as is generally regarded, John’s Gospel was written long after James’s death.
*See also* [John, The Apostle](dictionary:JohntheApostle).

Babylonian king who was co-regent with Nabonidus in the final days of the Babylonian Empire. His name means “Bel protect the king.” Daniel identifies him as the son of Nebuchadnezzar ([Dn 5:2, 11, 13, 18](Dan.5.2 Dan.5.11 Dan.5.13 Dan.5.18)), though in fact he was the natural son of Nabunaid (Nabonidus). The seeming discrepancy arises from the fact that in Hebrew literature “father” may signify “ancestor” or “predecessor,” and “son” may designate “descendant” or “successor in office.” Some have concluded that Belshazzar’s mother was a daughter of Nebuchadnezzar and that Belshazzar was therefore the grandson of the great Babylonian. Clearly his father, Nabunaid, was the son of a nobleman and the high priestess of the moon god at Haran. Nabunaid had usurped the throne in 555 BC.

A greater difficulty in the biblical text is the fact that Daniel presents Belshazzar as the king of Babylon when it fell to the Persians, whereas secular historical records picture Nabunaid as the last king of the Babylonian Empire. Critical scholars have therefore questioned Daniel’s accuracy. Inscriptions have now been found, however, which make it clear that Belshazzar’s father entrusted the rule of the capital to him and was out of the city for over 10 years campaigning in Arabia. Religious concerns also took Nabunaid out of Babylon during part of his reign. When Cyrus invaded the Babylonian Empire, Nabunaid marched east to meet him but fled before Cyrus’s advancing armies. Later he returned to Babylon and surrendered to the Persians after the city had already fallen to Cyrus. Thus he was out of the city when the Persians overcame the royal forces there under the command of Belshazzar, the crown prince and co-regent.

While Nabunaid’s armies were being routed by the Persians, Belshazzar was giving a sensual feast for the leaders of Babylonian society. Half drunk, he called for the gold and silver vessels from the Jerusalem temple to be brought in for use in a deliberate act of sacrilege. Immediately handwriting appeared on the wall, his doom was announced, and Persian armies entered the city without a fight (October 12, 539 BC). They did so by diverting the waters of the Euphrates so the river would no longer serve as a moat around the city and its defenses could be easily breached. *See* [Daniel, Book of](dictionary:DanielBookof); [Babylon, Babylonia](dictionary:BabylonBabylonia).

Daniel’s Babylonian name ([Dn 1:7](Dan.1.7)). Daniel was one of the young men taken captive to Babylon to be trained as counselors for King Nebuchadnezzar (ch [1](Dan.1.1-Dan.1.21)). *See* [Daniel (Person) #3](dictionary:DanielPerson).

Greek term for a judgment seat or tribunal of a Roman official. Although the term also means “to step” or “stride,” it was used in the first century AD primarily to denote an elevated area or platform (reached by steps) from which political orations or judicial decisions were made. Excavations in the city of Corinth have revealed a large, elaborately decorated *bema* located in the center of the marketplace.

In the NT, Jesus was questioned before the judgment seat of Pilate ([Mt 27:19](Matt.27.19); [Jn 19:13](John.19.13)). Herod Agrippa I addressed the people of Tyre and Sidon from a *bema* ([Acts 12:21](Acts.12.21)). The apostle Paul was brought before the tribunal of Gallio in Corinth ([18:12-17](Acts.18.12-Acts.18.17)) and again before Festus’s tribunal in Caesarea ([25:6, 10, 17](Acts.25.6 Acts.25.10 Acts.25.17)).

In two passages, Paul used the term to refer to God’s judgment seat. In [Romans 14:10](Rom.14.10) he warned those who would arrogantly judge others that all must stand before the tribunal of God. According to [2 Corinthians 5:10](2Cor.5.10), the merits of each person’s work will be determined before the judgment seat of Christ (cf. [1 Cor 3:13-15](1Cor.3.13-1Cor.3.15)).
*See also* [Judgment](dictionary:Judgment); [Judgment Seat](dictionary:JudgmentSeat); [Last Judgment](dictionary:LastJudgment).
Hebrew word often used as a prefix to describe a relationship. Literally meaning “son,” it is found some 4,850 times in the OT. The Aramaic equivalent is *bar* (see [Mt 16:17](Matt.16.17)).
*See also* [Bar](dictionary:Bar).

Levite musician appointed by King David ([1 Chr 15:18](1Chr.15.18), KJV). The Masoretic Text (the OT as annotated by medieval Hebrew scholars) and the KJV include the name Ben, but the Septuagint (ancient Greek translation of the OT) and modern versions omit it because it is missing in verses [20](1Chr.15.20) and [21](1Chr.15.21). Since the Masoretic Text also omits it in the later verses, the inclusion of Ben in verse [18](1Chr.15.18) may be a scribal error.

One of 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household. His administrative district comprised the area around Naphath-dor, the coastal city south of Mt Carmel ([1 Kgs 4:11](1Kgs.4.11)). The name means “son of Abinadab” and probably indicates that Ben-abinadab was the son of Solomon’s uncle Abinadab ([1 Sm 16:8](1Sam.16.8); [1 Chr 2:13](1Chr.2.13)).
Popular name meaning “the Lord has built,” used primarily by Levites.

1. Son of Jehoiada the priest, from the south Judean town of Kabzeel. Benaiah was engaged in military service, and his loyalty gained for him the rank of commander in chief of the army during the reign of Solomon ([1 Kgs 2:35](1Kgs.2.35); [4:4](1Kgs.4.4)).

Before David became king, Benaiah distinguished himself in a number of daring military and protective feats to become one of the mighty men ([2 Sm 23:20-22](2Sam.23.20-2Sam.23.22)) during David’s flight from King Saul. He attained command of “the thirty” ([1 Chr 27:6](1Chr.27.6)), a group second only to “the three” of highest valor ([2 Sm 23:23](2Sam.23.23)). He later had a high place in the armed forces when Joab was commander in chief and was placed over King David’s elite troops, the Cherethites and Pelethites ([8:18](2Sam.8.18)). He was also made third commander by David, with 24,000 men under him, and with annual responsibility for priestly service in the temple during the third month of the year ([1 Chr 27:5-6](1Chr.27.5-1Chr.27.6)).

Benaiah stayed loyal to David during the rebellion of Absalom ([2 Sm 20:23](2Sam.20.23); see [15:18](2Sam.15.18)) as well as during the attempt by Adonijah to seize David’s throne ([1 Kgs 1:8](1Kgs.1.8)), and therefore had the privilege of assisting in Solomon’s coronation at Gihon (vv [32-40](1Kgs.1.32-1Kgs.1.40)). As army commander and chief bodyguard to Solomon he was responsible for executing Adonijah ([2:25](1Kgs.2.25)), Joab (v [34](1Kgs.2.34)), and Shimei (v [46](1Kgs.2.46)) by orders of the new king.

2. Warrior from the town of Pirathon who was among David’s mighty men known as “the thirty” ([2 Sm 23:30](2Sam.23.30); [1 Chr 11:31](1Chr.11.31)). Benaiah commanded the 11th division of the army in the rotation system established by David ([1 Chr 27:14](1Chr.27.14)).
3. Prince in Simeon’s tribe who participated in the conquest of Gedor during Hezekiah’s reign ([1 Chr 4:36](1Chr.4.36)).

4. Levitical musician who played the harp when King David brought the ark to Jerusalem ([1 Chr 15:18, 20](1Chr.15.18 1Chr.15.20); [16:5](1Chr.16.5), RSV). Afterward, he was appointed to minister daily before the ark under the direction of Asaph ([16:5](1Chr.16.5)).

5. Priestly musician who blew the trumpet before the ark when King David brought it to Jerusalem ([1 Chr 15:24](1Chr.15.24)). Afterward he was appointed to play regularly before the ark ([16:6](1Chr.16.6)).
6. Father of Jehoiada, King David’s counselor after the death of Ahithophel ([1 Chr 27:34](1Chr.27.34); see also [2 Sm 17:1-14](2Sam.17.1-2Sam.17.14)).

7. Levite Asaph’s descendant and grandfather of Jahaziel ([2 Chr 20:14](2Chr.20.14)). Jahaziel delivered an encouraging prophecy to King Jehoshaphat of Judah before his battle against the Moabites and Ammonites (vv [1-29](2Chr.20.1-2Chr.20.29)).
8. Levite appointed by King Hezekiah to help oversee the tithes and contributions brought to the temple ([2 Chr 31:13](2Chr.31.13)).
9. Parosh’s son (or descendant), who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the Babylonian exile ([Ezr 10:25](Ezra.10.25)).
10. Pahath-moab’s son (or descendant), who also obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile ([Ezr 10:30](Ezra.10.30)).
11. Bani’s son (or descendant), another who divorced his pagan wife after the exile ([Ezr 10:35](Ezra.10.35)).
12. Nebo’s son (or descendant), who also divorced his pagan wife after the exile ([Ezr 10:43](Ezra.10.43)).
13. Pelatiah’s father ([Ez 11:1, 13](Ezek.11.1 Ezek.11.13)). Pelatiah was a prince of the people of Israel during the time of the prophet Ezekiel.

Son born to Lot and his younger daughter. A similar incestuous liaison between Lot and his older daughter produced a son named Moab. The two sons are identified as the ancestral heads of the Ammonite and Moabite peoples ([Gn 19:38](Gen.19.38)).

Although the promise made to Abraham could have been enjoyed by Lot ([Gn 11:31](Gen.11.31); [12:1-4](Gen.12.1-Gen.12.4)), Lot went his own way ([13:2-12](Gen.13.2-Gen.13.12)) and failed to trust the Lord ([19:15-23](Gen.19.15-Gen.19.23)). Lot’s relationship to Abraham, however, evoked deferential treatment by the Israelites ([Dt 2:8-19](Deut.2.8-Deut.2.19)) toward these occasionally powerful enemies ([2 Chr 20:1-12](2Chr.20.1-2Chr.20.12)).
*See also* [Ammon, Ammonites](dictionary:AmmonAmmonites).

One of 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household ([1 Kgs 4:9](1Kgs.4.9), KJV “son of Dekar”). Ben-deker’s administrative district comprised an area along the southern border of Dan’s tribe near Beth-shemesh.
One of the cities of Dan ([Jos 19:45](Josh.19.45)). The modern name is Ibn Ibrak, a suburb northwest of Tel Aviv.

Pronouncement of God’s favor upon an assembled congregation ([Gn 27:27-29](Gen.27.27-Gen.27.29); [Lk 24:50](Luke.24.50); [2 Cor 13:11, 14](2Cor.13.11 2Cor.13.14)). *See* [Bless, Blessing](dictionary:BlessBlessing).
Place where Israel camped near Edom’s border ([Nm 33:31-32](Num.33.31-Num.33.32)). *See* [Beeroth Bene-jaakan](dictionary:BeerothBeneJaakan).

Literally, “Geber’s son,” an official in King Solomon’s court who administered the sixth of 12 districts. Ben-geber’s area of responsibility began at Ramoth-gilead in northern Transjordan and extended north as far as Argob in Bashan ([1 Kgs 4:13](1Kgs.4.13)). His identification with Geber, son of Uri (v [19](1Kgs.4.19)), is debatable.
Title of two or possibly three kings of Syria, meaning “son of Hadad.” Hadad was the Syrian storm god probably identical with Rimmon ([2 Kgs 5:18](2Kgs.5.18)).

1. Ben-hadad I, son of Tabrimmon and grandson of Hezion. In spite of a history of Syrian hostility to Israel, Ben-hadad I entered into an alliance with King Baasha (908–886 BC) of the northern kingdom of Israel ([1 Kgs 15:18-20](1Kgs.15.18-1Kgs.15.20)). The pact was broken, however, when continuing hostilities between Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah erupted into a major encounter. Baasha conducted a major campaign against King Asa (910–869 BC) of Judah. In order to cut off infiltration into his kingdom and defection to the southern kingdom, Baasha fortified the city of Ramah, situated north of Jerusalem but uncomfortably close to it. His action extended Israel’s territory into Judah.

In the face of that threat, Asa sent his remaining wealth to Ben-hadad I, asking him to break his pact with Baasha (vv [18-19](1Kgs.15.18-1Kgs.15.19)). The Syrian king took advantage of the offer and sent his armies against Israel. He conquered the cities of Ijon, Dan, and Abel-beth-maacah plus the territory of Naphtali (v [20](1Kgs.15.20)), thus ensuring Syrian control of the main caravan routes through Galilee. Baasha was forced to abandon Ramah and move to Tirzah. Asa then conscripted the population of Judah to dismantle and carry off the fortifications erected by Baasha. Materials taken from Ramah were used to help build Geba in the territory of Benjamin. Asa’s victory became the subject of a prophetic protest by Hanani, who berated Asa for his reliance on the king of Syria ([16:7](1Kgs.16.7)).

2. Ben-hadad II. The biblical accounts in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles do not make a clear differentiation between Ben-hadad I and II. Some scholars have therefore identified them as a single person. This view finds apparent support in the “Melqart Stele,” which mentions Ben-hadad and to which a date of about 850 BC has been assigned. It seems better, however, to posit a Ben-hadad II who was the son of Ben-hadad I. If one does not distinguish between the two, Ben-hadad’s activity must overlap both the reign of Ahab (874–853 BC) and that of Baasha. In each, a military encounter with Ben-hadad was recorded; one must posit an interval of up to four decades between the encounters if no distinction is made.

Ben-hadad II led a coalition of armies against Samaria during the reign of King Ahab of Israel. In the course of the siege, Ben-hadad demanded that Ahab surrender his wealth, wives, and children to him. Ahab agreed to that demand, but when Ben-hadad added the condition that he be given anything that his aides laid their hands on, Ahab refused on advice of his counselors. His refusal enraged Ben-hadad.

An anonymous prophet predicted that Ahab would defeat the armies of Ben-hadad ([1 Kgs 20:13](1Kgs.20.13)). Ahab’s victory came when aides of the district governors killed the soldiers who had come out of the Syrian camp to take them captive. The Syrian forces fled. Ben-hadad was again defeated by the Israelites the next year when he attempted to engage them in battle on the plain rather than in the hill country. His reason was his belief that the “gods” of the Israelites were gods of the hills (v [23](1Kgs.20.23)). That Syrian defeat was also predicted by a prophet, who declared its cause to be Ben-hadad’s misconception of the nature of Israel’s God (v [28](1Kgs.20.28)).

Ben-hadad pleaded for his life, promising to restore all the cities his father had taken from Israel. Ahab agreed, but his action met with prophetic protest (vv [35-43](1Kgs.20.35-1Kgs.20.43)). The pact established by the two kings brought about a cessation of hostilities that lasted only three years. The peace was broken by Ahab, who, at the instigation of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, sought to regain the city of Ramoth-gilead. Guidance was first sought from a group of prophets who predicted victory. Micaiah, however, a true prophet, predicted defeat ([22:5-28](1Kgs.22.5-1Kgs.22.28)). Ahab’s forces were defeated, and Ahab died in battle (vv [29-36](1Kgs.22.29-1Kgs.22.36)).
Ben-hadad also figured in the life of the prophet Elisha, whom he sought to capture ([2 Kgs 6:11-19](2Kgs.6.11-2Kgs.6.19)). The attempt was thwarted when the Syrian army was stricken with blindness.

3. Ben-hadad III, son of King Hazael of Syria. This Ben-hadad was not related to Ben-hadad I or II but adopted the name. Because Jehoahaz (814–798 BC), king of Israel, did not follow the Lord, God allowed Israel to come under the control of Ben-hadad III. Release from the oppression of Ben-hadad III was accomplished by a “savior” ([2 Kgs 13:5](2Kgs.13.5)), probably a reference to Assyrian incursions into Syria.
*See also* [Syria, Syrians](dictionary:SyriaSyrians); [Israel, History of](dictionary:IsraelHistoryof).
One of five officials sent out by King Jehoshaphat of the southern kingdom of Judah to teach the people the law of the Lord ([2 Chr 17:7](2Chr.17.7)).
Shimon’s son of Judah’s tribe ([1 Chr 4:20](1Chr.4.20)).

One of the 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household ([1 Kgs 4:10](1Kgs.4.10), KJV “son of Hesed”). His administrative district comprised an area south and west of Arubboth in the western part of Manasseh’s tribe.
One of 12 officers appointed to requisition food for King Solomon’s household ([1 Kgs 4:8](1Kgs.4.8), KJV “son of Hur”). His district was the hill country of Ephraim.
Levite who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile ([Neh 10:13](Neh.10.13)).

1. Youngest of Jacob’s 12 sons and full brother to Joseph. Jacob named him Benjamin (“son of my right hand”) after his dying mother Rachel had called him Ben-oni (“son of my sorrow,” [Gn 35:18](Gen.35.18)). After Joseph had been sold into Egypt by his half brothers, their father, Jacob, assumed that Joseph was dead and became very protective of Benjamin. Later, with Joseph controlling the plot, Benjamin was used in the reunion in Egypt of Jacob and his 12 sons ([Gn 42–45](Gen.42.1-Gen.45.28)). When prophesying concerning each of his sons, Jacob spoke of Benjamin’s skill as a warrior or prophesied of the military fame of his descendants by saying, “Benjamin is a wolf that prowls. He devours his enemies in the morning, and in the evening he divides the plunder” ([49:27](Gen.49.27), NLT). *See* [Benjamin, Tribe of](dictionary:BenjaminTribeof).
2. Bilhan’s son and Jacob’s great-grandson ([1 Chr 7:10](1Chr.7.10)).
3. Member of Harim’s clan of the postexilic community who married a pagan wife ([Ezr 10:32](Ezra.10.32)).
4. One who repaired a section of the wall next to his own house ([Neh 3:23](Neh.3.23)).
5. One of the company of Jews who participated in the dedication of the wall at Jerusalem ([Neh 12:34](Neh.12.34)). He may be the same as #4 above.

One of the gates in Jerusalem’s old wall. The Gate of Benjamin was probably at the northeast corner, since the prophet Jeremiah passed through it on his way to Benjamin’s territory northeast of Jerusalem ([Jer 37:12-13](Jer.37.12-Jer.37.13)). On at least one occasion King Zedekiah held court there ([38:7](Jer.38.7)). It was essentially opposite the west wall’s Corner Gate ([Zec 14:10](Zech.14.10)). When the walls of Jerusalem were rebuilt at the end of the exile, a new gate known as the Sheep Gate ([Neh 3:1, 32](Neh.3.1 Neh.3.32)) or possibly the Muster Gate ([Neh 3:31](Neh.3.31)) may have been at the same site. *See* [Jerusalem](dictionary:Jerusalem).

One of the smallest of the 12 tribes of Israel, made up of descendants of Jacob’s youngest son ([Nm 1:36](Num.1.36)). In the OT the tribe is often referred to as simply “Benjamin.” Though small, the tribe of Benjamin played an important role in Israelite history, particularly in their conduct as great warriors ([Jgs 20:13-16](Judg.20.13-Judg.20.16); [1 Chr 12:1-2](1Chr.12.1-1Chr.12.2)).

At the Israelite conquest of Canaan, after the tribes of Judah and Ephraim had received their territory, the first lot came to Benjamin. The tribe was allotted territory between Judah and Ephraim, a strip of land between Mt Ephraim and the Judean hills. The southern boundary with Judah was clearly defined: through the valley of Hinnom immediately south of Jerusalem to a point north of the Dead Sea. Its eastern limit was the Jordan, and its northern boundary with Ephraim ran from the Jordan to Bethel to Ataroth-addar south of Lower Beth-horon ([Jos 18:11-20](Josh.18.11-Josh.18.20)).

Benjamin’s territory extended about 28 miles (45.1 kilometers) from west to east and 12 miles (19.3 kilometers) north to south. It was hilly country, strategically located to control key passes, but with fertile hill basins. Among its hill settlements were the important towns of Jerusalem, Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, Gibeah, and Mizpeh ([Jos 18:21-28](Josh.18.21-Josh.18.28)). Not all of its towns were immediately taken from their previous possessors; Jerusalem, for example, was in the hands of the Jebusites until David’s time. The environment bred a hardy race of highlanders, well described in Jacob’s blessing of Benjamin as “a wolf that prowls” ([Gn 49:27](Gen.49.27)).

Ehud of Benjamin was one of the early judges in Canaan, a “deliverer” of the Israelites who killed Eglon, king of Moab ([Jgs 3:15](Judg.3.15)). Members of the tribe later helped Deborah and Barak defeat Sisera ([5:14](Judg.5.14)). The tribe continued to produce great men: political leaders ([1 Chr 27:21](1Chr.27.21)), captains in Saul’s army ([2 Sm 4:2](2Sam.4.2)) and David’s army ([23:29](2Sam.23.29)), skilled archers ([1 Chr 8:40](1Chr.8.40)), and overseers in Solomon’s labor force ([1 Kgs 4:18](1Kgs.4.18)).

Less noble traits were also shown by Benjamin’s descendants. Palti, a Benjaminite, was one of the scouts making a bad report when the 12 spies returned from the land of Canaan ([Nm 13:1-2, 9, 31-33](Num.13.1-Num.13.2 Num.13.9 Num.13.31-Num.13.33)). The tribe as a whole displayed disobedience and lack of consistent courage by failing to clear their inheritance of Canaanites ([Jgs 1:21](Judg.1.21)). Following the custom of the day, the whole tribe defended the lewd treatment and murder of a concubine from another tribe by a few of their members (chs [19–20](Judg.19.1-Judg.20.48)). That act of gross immorality united the other tribes against them, and the tribe of Benjamin was almost decimated. To keep the tribe from dying out, the other tribes allowed the Benjaminites to take captive several hundred women who then became their wives ([Jgs 21](Judg.21.1-Judg.21.25)).

Benjamin’s tribe proved to be dependable in various ways. During the exodus from Egypt, it took its place in the organization ([Nm 1:11](Num.1.11)) and the army ([2:22](Num.2.22)) and made its tribal offerings ([7:60](Num.7.60)). It demonstrated remarkable loyalty to the throne, initially to Saul and his family ([2 Sm 2:8-31](2Sam.2.8-2Sam.2.31)). Later David received its faithful support, as did his descendants, for Benjamin remained with Judah, loyal to Solomon’s son Rehoboam when Jeroboam led a secession ([1 Kgs 12:21-24](1Kgs.12.21-1Kgs.12.24)).

Other men of Benjamin (often called Benjaminites) spoken of in the OT include Cush, of whom David sang ([Ps 7](Ps.7.1-Ps.7.17) superscription); Jeremiah the prophet, who, though a Levite, lived within Benjamin’s tribe ([Jer 1:1](Jer.1.1); [32:8](Jer.32.8)); and Mordecai, uncle and adviser to Queen Esther ([Est 2:5](Esth.2.5)).

In the NT the apostle Paul made no apologies for his ancestry, twice referring to himself as a Hebrew of Benjamin’s tribe ([Rom 11:1](Rom.11.1); [Phil 3:5](Phil.3.5)). In his sermon at Antioch of Pisidia, Paul also mentioned Benjamin as the tribe of King Saul, in his brief account of Israel’s history ([Acts 13:21](Acts.13.21)). In one other NT reference Benjamin is named with the other 11 tribes in John’s apocalyptic vision ([Rv 7:8](Rev.7.8)). *See* [Benjamin (Person) #1](dictionary:BenjaminPerson).
Member of Benjamin’s tribe. *See* [Benjamin, Tribe of](dictionary:BenjaminTribeof).

Jaaziah’s son in a list of Levites assigned to temple duty ([1 Chr 24:26-27](1Chr.24.26-1Chr.24.27)). It is possible that the Hebrew word is not a proper name; it has sometimes been translated “his son.”

Name Rachel gave to her last son as she died in childbirth ([Gn 35:18](Gen.35.18)). His father, Jacob, changed his name from Ben-oni (“son of my sorrow”) to Benjamin (“son of my right hand”). *See* [Benjamin (Person) #1](dictionary:BenjaminPerson).
Son of Sirach and author of Wisdom of Jesus ben Sirach (also known as Ecclesiasticus). *See* [Wisdom of Jesus ben Sirach](dictionary:WisdomofJesusBenSirach).
Ishi’s son from Judah’s tribe ([1 Chr 4:20](1Chr.4.20)).
Alternate name for Baal-meon, a city east of the Jordan, in [Numbers 32:3](Num.32.3). *See* [Baal-meon](dictionary:BaalMeon).
1. Bela’s father ([Gn 36:32](Gen.36.32)). Bela was a king of Edom.
2. Balaam’s father ([Nm 22:5](Num.22.5); [2 Pt 2:15](2Pet.2.15), KJV “Bosor”). Balaam was asked by Balak, king of Moab, to curse Israel.
Ruler of Sodom in the days of Abraham and Lot. Bera was one of five Canaanite city kings who unsuccessfully rebelled against King Chedorlaomer of Elam and his three allies ([Gn 14:2](Gen.14.2)).
Warrior from Benjamin’s tribe who joined David at Ziklag in his struggle against King Saul. Beracah was one of David’s ambidextrous archers and slingers ([1 Chr 12:3](1Chr.12.3)).

Place where King Jehoshaphat gathered the people of Judah to praise the Lord ([2 Chr 20:26](2Chr.20.26)). The people were grateful for God’s help in defeating the attacking armies of Moab, Ammon, and Mt Seir ([2 Chr 20:1-25](2Chr.20.1-2Chr.20.25)). It is most often identified with the area Wadi el ’Arrub, not far from Tekoa, where a ruin called Bereikut exists.
KJV spelling of Berechiah, Asaph’s father, in [1 Chronicles 6:39](1Chr.6.39). *See* [Berechiah #2](dictionary:Berechiah).
One of Shimei’s sons from Benjamin’s tribe ([1 Chr 8:21](1Chr.8.21)).
1. Place north of Jerusalem where the Syrian army camped before launching an attack that killed Judas Maccabeus in 161 BC (1 Macc 9:4).

2. Ancient city of Macedonia (a region now divided among Greece, Yugoslavia, and Bulgaria), probably founded in the fifth century BC. The city was approximately 25 miles (40.2 kilometers) inland from the Aegean Sea on a scenic and fertile plain 600 feet (182.8 kilometers) high in the foothills north of the Olympian range. Conquered by Rome in 168 BC, Berea (alternately spelled Beroea in older English translations) was one of the most populous Macedonian cities in the time of Christ. Today the city is known as Verria.

Berea was visited by the apostle Paul on his second missionary journey ([Acts 17:10-15](Acts.17.10-Acts.17.15)) and was the home of Sopater, Paul’s companion ([Acts 20:4](Acts.20.4)). Paul and Silas left Thessalonica when violent religious and political opposition arose and went to Berea, 50 miles (80.5 kilometers) southwest. There both Jews and Greeks eagerly received the gospel, but Paul had to leave the city when angry Jews arrived from Thessalonica to stir up trouble.
1. Son of Zerubbabel and descendant of King David ([1 Chr 3:20](1Chr.3.20)).
2. Levite, Gershon’s descendant and father of Asaph ([1 Chr 6:39](1Chr.6.39); [15:17](1Chr.15.17)). Asaph was a famous musician of Israel.
3. Asa’s son and head of a family of Levites who returned to Judah after the Babylonian exile ([1 Chr 9:16](1Chr.9.16)).
4. Levite appointed by King David as gatekeeper for the ark of the covenant ([1 Chr 15:23](1Chr.15.23)).

5. Meshillemoth’s son, a leader of Ephraim’s tribe. He was one of three men in Samaria who supported the prophet Obed in sending prisoners of war back to their homes in Judah ([2 Chr 28:12](2Chr.28.12)).
6. Meshullam’s father. Meshullam assisted Nehemiah, the governor, in rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem ([Neh 3:4, 30](Neh.3.4 Neh.3.30); [6:18](Neh.6.18)).
7. Iddo’s son and father of Zechariah the prophet ([Zec 1:1, 7](Zech.1.1 Zech.1.7)).
*See also* [Barachiah, Barachias](dictionary:BarachiahBarachias).
Alternate name for Beker, one of Ephraim’s sons, in [1 Chronicles 7:20](1Chr.7.20). *See* [Beker, Bekerite #2](dictionary:BekerBekerite).
Unknown site in Israel’s southern Negev Desert region. God spoke to Sarai’s maid, Hagar, at a well between Kadesh and Bered ([Gn 16:14](Gen.16.14)).
Alternate spelling for Berechiah. *See* [Berechiah](dictionary:Berechiah).
Zophah’s son, head of a subclan. Beri was a skilled warrior ([1 Chr 7:36, 40](1Chr.7.36 1Chr.7.40)) listed with Asher’s descendants.
1. Asher’s son, who migrated to Egypt with his family, relatives, and grandfather Jacob ([Gn 46:17](Gen.46.17); [1 Chr 7:30](1Chr.7.30)). His descendants were called Beriites ([Nm 26:44](Num.26.44)).
2. Ephraim’s youngest son, born after several of his brothers were killed at Gath for cattle rustling ([1 Chr 7:20-23](1Chr.7.20-1Chr.7.23)).
3. Elpaal’s son, head of a family in Benjamin’s tribe. This Beriah lived at Aijalon and helped repel invaders from Gath ([1 Chr 8:13](1Chr.8.13)).

4. Shimei’s son, a Levite of Gershon’s clan who served in the temple at Jerusalem. Because neither Beriah nor his brother Jeush had many sons, their families were counted as a single subclan in the Levitical system ([1 Chr 23:10-11](1Chr.23.10-1Chr.23.11)).
Member of a family descended from Beriah, one of Asher’s sons ([Nm 26:44](Num.26.44)). *See* [Beriah #1](dictionary:Beriah).
KJV rendering of Bichrite, a descendant of Bichri, in [2 Samuel 20:14](2Sam.20.14). *See* [Bichri, Bichrite, Bicri](dictionary:BichriBichriteBicri).

Eldest daughter of Herod Agrippa I. Bernice was present during the apostle Paul’s speech before her brother King Agrippa II ([Acts 25:13, 23](Acts.25.13 Acts.25.23); [26:30](Acts.26.30)). Bernice (also spelled Berenice) was born around AD 28. At 13 she married Marcus, son of the Jewish official Alexander. After her husband’s death, her father betrothed her to his elder brother, Herod of Chalcis. Two sons, Bernicianus and Hyrcanus, were born to them before her second husband’s death in AD 48. When the young widow’s relationship with her brother, Agrippa II, deepened, there were rumors of incest. In defense, Bernice persuaded Polemo, king of Cilicia, to marry her. But she left him shortly afterward.

In AD 66 Bernice bravely but unsuccessfully appealed to the mad Roman procurator Gessius Florus not to ransack the temple in Jerusalem. She was at her brother’s side when he warned the people against war. When war broke out that year, Jewish rebels set fire to her palace as well as to her brother’s.
KJV spelling of Merodach-baladan, the king of Babylon during the reign of Judah’s King Hezekiah, in [2 Kings 20:12](2Kgs.20.12). *See* [Merodach-baladan](dictionary:MerodachBaladan).
*See* [Berea #2](dictionary:Berea).

City between Damascus and Hamath mentioned by the prophet Ezekiel as lying on the northern border of the restored Israel ([Ez 47:16](Ezek.47.16)). Berothah is probably the same as Berothai, a city captured by David ([2 Sm 8:8](2Sam.8.8); called Cun in [1 Chr 18:8](1Chr.18.8)).
KJV form of Beerothite, an inhabitant of Beeroth, in [1 Chronicles 11:39](1Chr.11.39). *See* [Beeroth](dictionary:Beeroth).
Fleshy fruit, usually with many seeds and having no stony seed covering. *See* [Plants (Bramble](dictionary:Plants); [Caper Plant)](dictionary:CaperPlant).

Hard, lustrous mineral of various colors, mentioned in the Bible as a gemstone ([Ex 28:20](Exod.28.20); [Rv 21:20](Rev.21.20)). *See* [Minerals and Metals](dictionary:MineralsandMetals); [Stones, Precious](dictionary:StonesPrecious).
Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile ([Ezr 2:49](Ezra.2.49); [Neh 7:52](Neh.7.52)).
Meshullam’s father. Along with Joiada, Meshullam helped rebuild a portion of the Jerusalem wall after the exile in Babylonia ([Neh 3:6](Neh.3.6)).

Old English word meaning “broom” ([Is 14:23](Isa.14.23), KJV). The besom, or broom, of destruction is a Near Eastern metaphor signifying total destruction. It refers to the annihilation or “sweeping away” of Babylon by the Lord.

Brook that David crossed to pursue the Amalekites southward after they had raided Ziklag, his home base. Exhausted, 200 of David’s men remained at the brook while the other 400 overtook and defeated the enemy ([1 Sm 30:9-21](1Sam.30.9-1Sam.30.21)).
Alternate name for Tibhath ([1 Chr 18:8](1Chr.18.8)), a town in the city-kingdom of Aram-zobah, subjugated by King David, in [2 Samuel 8:8](2Sam.8.8). *See* [Tebah (Place)](dictionary:TebahPlace).
City allotted to Asher’s tribe for an inheritance, mentioned between Hali and Achshaph ([Jos 19:25](Josh.19.25)).

Village where messengers from the Pharisees questioned John the Baptist ([Jn 1:28](John.1.28), KJV). Modern translations have “Bethany” instead of Bethabara in accordance with superior manuscript evidence. John called it Bethany “beyond the Jordan” to distinguish it from the Bethany near Jerusalem. *See* [Bethany #2](dictionary:Bethany).

Town assigned to Naphtali’s tribe ([Jos 19:38](Josh.19.38)) from which the tribe failed to drive out the original inhabitants ([Jgs 1:33](Judg.1.33)). The Israelites, who often made slaves of the remaining Canaanite people, were in many cases eventually corrupted by their pagan religious practices.
Village in the hill country assigned to Judah’s tribe after the Israelite conquest of Canaan ([Jos 15:59](Josh.15.59)).

1. Village on the eastern slope of the Mt of Olives about a mile and a half (2.4 kilometers) east of Jerusalem. Jesus and his disciples sometimes stayed in Bethany when in Judea, as when they attended temple observances during Passover ([Mt 21:17](Matt.21.17); [Mk 11:11](Mark.11.11)). Jesus was eating at the home of Simon the leper in Bethany when a woman came and anointed his head with costly perfume ([Mt 26:6-13](Matt.26.6-Matt.26.13); [Mk 14:3-9](Mark.14.3-Mark.14.9)). Bethany was also the home of Mary and Martha and their brother Lazarus, where Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead ([Jn 11:1, 18](John.11.1 John.11.18)). The village was near Bethphage on an approach to Jerusalem ([Mk 11:1](Mark.11.1); [Lk 19:29](Luke.19.29)) that Jesus followed in preparation for his triumphal entry into Jerusalem. In Bethany Jesus blessed his disciples after the resurrection and parted from them ([Lk 24:50](Luke.24.50)). Today the town is called el-Azariyeh (the place of Lazarus).
2. Village on “the other side of the Jordan” (the east side), where John the Baptist baptized ([Jn 1:28](John.1.28)).

One of six cities in the wilderness southeast of Jericho on the boundary between the territories of Judah and Benjamin ([Jos 15:6, 61](Josh.15.6 Josh.15.61); [18:22](Josh.18.22)). The modern Ain Gharbeh in the Wadi el-Quelt may be the site of Beth-arabah.
KJV rendering of Beth-haram, a Gadite town, in [Joshua 13:27](Josh.13.27). *See* [Beth-haram, Beth-haran](dictionary:BethHaramBethHaran).

Town whose violent destruction at the hands of the Assyrians was compared by the prophet Hosea to Ephraim’s forthcoming destruction ([Hos 10:14](Hos.10.14)). Beth-arbel is most commonly identified with present-day Irbid in Gilead, located at an important crossroads in northern Transjordan.
Place where certain families descended from Judah were known for their production of linen ([1 Chr 4:21](1Chr.4.21)). The KJV renders “Ashbea” as a family name rather than a place of residence.

1. Town in Benjamin’s territory, located west of Michmash on the border of the wilderness, near Ai, to the east of Bethel ([Jos 7:2](Josh.7.2); [18:12](Josh.18.12); [1 Sm 13:5](1Sam.13.5); [14:23](1Sam.14.23)).

2. Term used by Hosea contemptuously to refer to Bethel, an ancient center of worship, because the “House of God” (Bethel) had become a “house of wickedness” (Beth-aven or just Aven; [Hos 4:15](Hos.4.15); [5:8](Hos.5.8); [10:5](Hos.10.5)). *See* [Aven #2](dictionary:Aven).
Alternate name for Azmaveth, a town near Jerusalem, in [Nehemiah 7:28](Neh.7.28). *See* [Azmaveth (Place)](dictionary:AzmavethPlace).
Alternate name for Baal-meon, a city in Reuben’s territory, in [Joshua 13:17](Josh.13.17). *See* [Baal-meon](dictionary:BaalMeon).
Place where warriors of Ephraim’s tribe under Gideon tried to block the retreat of the Midianites over the Jordan River ([Jgs 7:24](Judg.7.24)).

Town in the Judean wilderness where Jonathan and Simon Maccabeus took refuge from General Bacchides and, having fortified it successfully, withstood the onslaught of the Syrian forces (1 Macc 9:62-68). After that defeat Bacchides was forced to make peace with Jonathan (vv 69-73).
Alternate name for Lebaoth, a city in Judah’s southern territory ([1 Chr 4:31](1Chr.4.31)). *See* [Lebaoth](dictionary:Lebaoth).
Place in Benjamin’s territory to which a Philistine army was pursued by the Israelites after the second battle of Ebenezer ([1 Sm 7:11](1Sam.7.11)).

Shrine of the Philistine and Canaanite god Dagon mentioned in several sources other than the Bible. A fortress called Dagon near Jericho was mentioned by the Jewish historian Josephus, for example. Many Canaanite locations may have been known for their shrines to Dagon:
1. Town in Judah’s lowlands ([Jos 15:41](Josh.15.41)). This Beth-dagon was mentioned both by Ramses III of Egypt and by Sennacherib of Assyria (701 BC) as having been captured by them.
2. Town on the border of Asher’s territory, east of Mt Carmel ([Jos 19:27](Josh.19.27)).
3. Temple in Ashdod ([1 Sm 5:1-2](1Sam.5.1-1Sam.5.2); called Azotus in 1 Macc 10:83-84).
Town in Moab ([Jer 48:22](Jer.48.22)), and probably identical with Almon-diblathaim. *See* [Almon-diblathaim](dictionary:AlmonDiblathaim).

Small Aramean (Syrian) state north of Damascus. Assyria conquered Beth-eden and deported its people to Kir ([2 Kgs 16:9](2Kgs.16.9)), fulfilling the prediction in [Amos 1:5](Amos.1.5) (KJV “house of Eden”). Beth-eden, which means “house of delight,” is sometimes equated with the Eden of [Ezekiel 27:23](Ezek.27.23), the location of which is unknown. Its inhabitants are referred to as the “children of Eden” in [2 Kings 19:12](2Kgs.19.12) (KJV).
Place between Jezreel and Samaria where Jehu killed Ahaziah’s kinsmen at a pit or cistern ([2 Kgs 10:12, 14](2Kgs.10.12 2Kgs.10.14), KJV “shearing house”).

Pagan deity mentioned in ancient texts and thought by some to have biblical reference ([Jer 48:13](Jer.48.13); [Am 5:5](Amos.5.5); [Zec 7:2](Zech.7.2)). *See* [Canaanite Deities and Religion](dictionary:CanaaniteDeitiesandReligion).

1. Important OT city located about 11 miles (17.7 kilometers) north of Jerusalem on the north-south ridge road at the tribal borders of Benjamin and Ephraim ([Jos 16:1-2](Josh.16.1-Josh.16.2); [18:13](Josh.18.13)). Hiel, a resident of the city, is referred to as a Bethelite in [1 Kings 16:34](1Kgs.16.34) (KJV). As a trading center, Bethel attracted merchandise both from the Mediterranean coast and from Transjordan via Jericho. Although the site was located in dry hill country, several springs supplied ample water for its inhabitants (the oldest artifact recovered from the site is a water jar dating from about 3500 BC).

The name of Bethel, meaning “house of El (god),” may have been used as early as the fourth millennium BC by Canaanites in the area. Archaeological excavations at Chalcolithic levels (i.e., between the Stone Age and the Bronze Age) indicate that pagan worship of the Canaanite deity El took place on top of the hill at that early period. The patriarch Jacob named the place Bethel, or gave the old name new significance, after having a dream from God there ([Gn 28:10-22](Gen.28.10-Gen.28.22)). The site was said to be known as Bethel to the patriarch Abraham ([12:8](Gen.12.8)); that designation, however, could be a scribal updating of a more ancient local name, since Bethel had earlier been known as Luz ([28:19](Gen.28.19)). Possibly the sanctuary was known as Bethel, the nearby settlement as Luz. No doubt the name Bethel was firmly established by the beginning of the intermediate Bronze Age (c. 2200 BC) and remained throughout its history. An OT passage mentioning both names records that a man from Luz founded another city of that name in Hittite territory ([Jgs 1:26](Judg.1.26)).

Although Bethel was assigned to Benjamin’s tribe, Ephraim’s tribe actually captured Bethel from its Canaanite fortress in their own territory ([Jgs 1:22-26](Judg.1.22-Judg.1.26); [1 Chr 7:28](1Chr.7.28)). Under the judges, the ark of the covenant was located at Bethel, where the normal functions of Israelite worship were carried out; the ark was superintended by the high priest Phinehas, son of Eleazar ([Jgs 20:18-28](Judg.20.18-Judg.20.28); [21:2-4](Judg.21.2-Judg.21.4)). There is no archaeological evidence of Philistine occupation of Bethel in the time of the judges; in the days of King Saul it was bypassed when other Israelite centers were being attacked (cf. [1 Sm 12–14](1Sam.12.1-1Sam.14.52)). Archaeological discoveries indicate that Bethel flourished in the early reign of Saul but declined when he made Gibeah his capital city.

When Israel and Judah became separate entities in the time of Jeroboam I (930–909 BC), Bethel returned to prominence as the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, thus becoming the counterpart of Judah’s capital, Jerusalem. Bethel was one of two northern cities where golden calves were worshiped ([1 Kgs 12:28-33](1Kgs.12.28-1Kgs.12.33)); the sanctuary area for that cultic practice has not been discovered. The city was the home of an elderly prophet ([13:11](1Kgs.13.11)) who may have been connected with the prophetic colony existing there in the time of Elijah and Elisha ([2 Kgs 2:2-3](2Kgs.2.2-2Kgs.2.3)). During the reign of Judah’s King Abijah (913–910 BC), Bethel fell under Judah’s control ([2 Chr 13:19](2Chr.13.19)) but later was returned to Israel. The prophet Amos went to Bethel to deliver scathing denunciations about contemporary social and religious life in Israel, for which the priest Amaziah had him expelled ([Am 7:10-13](Amos.7.10-Amos.7.13)).

There is no archaeological evidence that Bethel was destroyed during the Assyrian conquest of Israel (722 BC). In fact, one of its deported priests was returned to Bethel to instruct Mesopotamian colonists in the ways of the Lord ([2 Kgs 17:28](2Kgs.17.28)).
