Under Hebrew law, it was a father’s duty to teach his son the means of earning a livelihood. Hammurabi’s code prescribed that an adopted son had to be similarly trained, and if in any way he was not reared as a natural child within the family, he might return to his own home.

If a man subsequently had a family of his own and the foster child was sent away, he had the right to take with him one-third of the man’s goods, although none of his land or his house, since these were the inheritance of the natural children. If a child died in a nurse’s care and she took another assignment without informing the new employers of the previous death, her breast was cut off.

The most famous section of Hammurabi’s law code concerns assault: “If a \[man\] has destroyed the eye of a member of the aristocracy, they shall destroy his eye.” Similarly, if he broke a man’s bone or knocked out a tooth, he would suffer the same fate (sections 196–197). If the injured person was a commoner, however, a fine of one mina of silver was charged for destroying an eye or breaking a bone. When the injured man was a slave, payment of half his value had to be made. Punishments for simple assault depended upon the rank of the two protagonists. Where a man swore that the blow was not deliberate, he might simply pay the physician’s bill. Other penalties were set out for instances where the blow was fatal or caused a woman to miscarry (sections 209–214).

Surgeons’ fees were also specified. For saving a life or for eye surgery, the fee was ten shekels of silver when the patient was an aristocrat, but only five for a commoner, and two for a slave. If an aristocratic patient died under the surgeon’s bronze knife, or lost an eye, the surgeon could have his hand cut off (section 218). If a slave died during surgery, the surgeon had to replace the slave with another. For setting a broken bone or healing a sprained tendon, the physician charged five, three, or two shekels, depending on the patient’s status (sections 221–223).

The final section of laws concerns the protection of people from the poor workmanship of house and boat builders, rules and regulations for those who rent animals or hire people, theft of agricultural implements, rates for hiring and paying wages, and rules for the purchase and sale of slaves (sections 228–282).

A man who fraudulently let out his master’s oxen for hire rather than using them on his own fields would be required to pay the normal rental of grain for the field. If he was unable to do so, he was to be dragged through that field by the oxen.

Because of similarities in culture, it is hardly surprising that there should be areas of correspondence between Hammurabi’s code and the Mosaic law. Thus both bodies of legislation prescribed the death penalty for adultery (Hammurabi section 129; [Lv 20:10](Lev.20.10); [Dt 22:22](Deut.22.22)) and for the kidnapping and selling of an individual (Hammurabi section 114; [Ex 21:16](Exod.21.16)). The *lex talionis,* or principle of retaliation, in [Exodus 21:23-25](Exod.21.23-Exod.21.25) and [Deuteronomy 19:21](Deut.19.21) is reflected widely in Hammurabi’s laws, including sections 197, 210, and 230. The differences, however, are equally significant. Whereas Hammurabi’s legislation allowed women equal rights of divorce (section 142), these were denied under the Mosaic law by simply not being included (cf. [Dt 24:1-4](Deut.24.1-Deut.24.4)). Hammurabi’s code was basically pragmatic in nature, and although promulgated under the authority of Shamash, god of justice, the legislation took little notice of ethical and spiritual principles.
*See also* [Civil Law and Justice](dictionary:CivilLawandJustice); [Criminal Law and Punishment](dictionary:CriminalLawandPunishment); [Law, Biblical Concept of](dictionary:LawBiblicalConceptof).
Name of site meaning “horde” in the Transjordan where the marauding armies of Gog will be destroyed by the Israelites ([Ez 39:16](Ezek.39.16)).
*See also* [Gog #2](dictionary:Gog).
Valley in the Transjordan where the dead of the armies of Gog (Gog’s “hordes”) will be buried ([Ez 39:11, 15](Ezek.39.11 Ezek.39.15)).

Hivite or Horite prince of the country about Shechem ([Gn 34:2](Gen.34.2)), from whom Jacob bought land when returning with his family from Paddan-aram. At this time Hamor’s son Shechem committed fornication with Dinah, the daughter of Jacob. At his son’s request Hamor asked Jacob for a marriage alliance between Shechem and Dinah, offering a dowry. Simeon and Levi, in pretended friendship, persuaded the males of the city to be circumcised, but then attacked and killed them before they were healed, taking revenge for their sister’s humiliation.

“Hamor” is the Hebrew word that Jacob uses to denote Issachar in blessing his sons ([Gn 49:14](Gen.49.14)) and is the usual word for “ass” in the OT (e.g., [Gn 42:26](Gen.42.26); [Ex 20:17](Exod.20.17); [Jgs 15:15](Judg.15.15); [Is 1:3](Isa.1.3); [Zec 9:9](Zech.9.9)).
Alternate name for Hemdan, Dishon’s oldest son in [1 Chronicles 1:41](1Chr.1.41) (see NLT mg). *See* [Hemdan](dictionary:Hemdan).
KJV spelling of Hammuel, the Simeonite, in [1 Chronicles 4:26](1Chr.4.26). *See* [Hammuel](dictionary:Hammuel).
Perez’s younger son ([Gn 46:12](Gen.46.12); [1 Chr 2:5](1Chr.2.5)) and founder of the Hamulite family ([Nm 26:21](Num.26.21)).
Daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, one of King Josiah’s wives, and the mother of two kings: Jehoahaz and Zedekiah ([2 Kgs 23:31](2Kgs.23.31); [24:18](2Kgs.24.18); [Jer 52:1](Jer.52.1)).

Shallum’s son, from whom Jeremiah bought a field in Anathoth ([Jer 32:7-12](Jer.32.7-Jer.32.12)). This purchase signified that God would restore the nation and that possession of the land would again be possible.
1. Shashak’s son and one of the chief men of Benjamin ([1 Chr 8:23](1Chr.8.23)).
2. Azel’s son from Benjamin’s tribe ([1 Chr 8:38](1Chr.8.38); [9:44](1Chr.9.44)).
3. Warrior among David’s mighty men, who were known as “the thirty” ([1 Chr 11:43](1Chr.11.43)).
4. Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Ezr 2:46](Ezra.2.46); [Neh 7:49](Neh.7.49)).
5. Levitical assistant who explained to the people passages from the law read by Ezra ([Neh 8:7](Neh.8.7)).
6. Levite who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile ([Neh 10:10](Neh.10.10)).
7, 8. Two political leaders who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile ([Neh 10:22, 26](Neh.10.22 Neh.10.26)).
9. One of the Levites whom Nehemiah appointed as treasurer over the storehouses ([Neh 13:13](Neh.13.13)).
10. Igdaliah’s son and head of a prophetic guild occupying the room in the temple where Jeremiah offered the Rechabites wine to drink ([Jer 35:4](Jer.35.4)).

Tower on the north wall of Jerusalem, located near the Sheep Gate ([Neh 3:1](Neh.3.1); [12:39](Neh.12.39); KJV “Hananeel”). Later in Israel’s history John Hyrcanus erected a Maccabean fortress on this spot, which Pompey destroyed in 63 BC. Still later, Herod the Great built the Tower of Antonia here to oversee the temple area. Two prophecies refer to the Tower of Hananel as a boundary point in the rebuilding of Jerusalem ([Jer 31:38](Jer.31.38); [Zec 14:10](Zech.14.10)).

1. Seer who rebuked King Asa for giving treasure to Ben-hadad of Syria to persuade him to attack Israel. Hanani was imprisoned for his preaching ([2 Chr 16:1-10](2Chr.16.1-2Chr.16.10)). Hanani was the father of the prophet Jehu, who made protests against Baasha, king of Israel ([1 Kgs 16:1-7](1Kgs.16.1-1Kgs.16.7)), and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah ([2 Chr 19:2](2Chr.19.2)).
2. Heman’s son, David’s seer, and a musician in the temple ([1 Chr 25:4, 25](1Chr.25.4 1Chr.25.25)).
3. Priest who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after returning from exile ([Ezr 10:20](Ezra.10.20)).

4. Brother of Nehemiah who induced him to act on behalf of the Jews when he reported the state of Jerusalem and Judah ([Neh 1:2](Neh.1.2)). Hanani was later given responsibility for the city of Jerusalem ([7:2](Neh.7.2)).
5. Priest and musician who participated in the dedication of the rebuilt walls of Jerusalem ([Neh 12:36](Neh.12.36)).
1. Zerubbabel’s son and a descendant of David ([1 Chr 3:19, 21](1Chr.3.19 1Chr.3.21)).
2. Benjamite and the son of Shashak ([1 Chr 8:24](1Chr.8.24)).
3. Heman’s son and the leader of the 16th of 24 divisions of musicians trained for service in the house of the Lord ([1 Chr 25:4, 23](1Chr.25.4 1Chr.25.23)).
4. One of the commanders of King Uzziah’s army ([2 Chr 26:11](2Chr.26.11)).
5. Bebai’s son, who returned with the exiles from Babylon and was later encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife ([Ezr 10:28](Ezra.10.28)).
6. Perfumer who helped Nehemiah rebuild the Jerusalem wall ([Neh 3:8](Neh.3.8)).
7. Shelemiah’s son, who with Hanun repaired a section of the Jerusalem wall during the days of Nehemiah ([Neh 3:30](Neh.3.30)). He is perhaps identical with #6 above.

8. Commander of the citadel of Jerusalem who was assigned by Nehemiah to rule the city jointly with Hanani, Nehemiah’s brother. Hananiah, described as a faithful and God-fearing man, was appointed the task of seeing that the city walls and gates were regularly guarded ([Neh 7:2-3](Neh.7.2-Neh.7.3)).
9. One of the leaders of the people who set his seal on the covenant of Ezra ([Neh 10:23](Neh.10.23)).
10. Head of the priestly family of Jeremiah during the days of Joiakim, the high priest, in postexilic Jerusalem ([Neh 12:12](Neh.12.12)).
11. One of the priests who blew a trumpet at the dedication of the Jerusalem wall during the days of Nehemiah ([Neh 12:41](Neh.12.41)).

12. Gibeonite and the son of Azzur. Hananiah prophesied during the fourth year of King Zedekiah of Judah’s reign (597–586 BC). He openly declared in the temple that in two years the Lord would break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon (605–562 BC), from the neck of Judah and return its exiles and sacred possessions to Palestine. Told by the Lord that Hananiah’s prophecy was false, Jeremiah reproached Hananiah for lying and foretold his imminent death. Hananiah died two months later ([Jer 28](Jer.28.1-Jer.28.17)).
13. Father of Zedekiah, an official of King Jehoiakim of Judah (609–598 BC; [Jer 36:12](Jer.36.12)).
14. Grandfather of Irijah, the captain of the guards, who arrested Jeremiah at Jerusalem’s Gate of Benjamin for apparently deserting to the Babylonians ([Jer 37:13](Jer.37.13)).
15. One of the three Jewish friends of Daniel exiled in Babylon. He was assigned the Babylonian name Shadrach ([Dn 1:6-19](Dan.1.6-Dan.1.19); [2:17](Dan.2.17)).
*See also* [Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego](dictionary:ShadrachMeshachandAbednego).

The terminal part of the forelimb that has the ability to grasp. “Hand” is used hundreds of times in the Bible to describe a physical part of one’s body. It is also used frequently in metaphors or figurative language.

Figuratively, the hand meant power ([Dt 2:15](Deut.2.15); [Ps 31:5](Ps.31.5); [Mk 14:62](Mark.14.62)). Indeed, in [Joshua 8:20](Josh.8.20) “hand to flee” is translated “power to flee” (see [Ps 76:5](Ps.76.5)). Conversely, limp hands symbolized irresoluteness and weakness ([Is 35:3](Isa.35.3)). Clasping the hands signified friendship ([2 Kgs 10:15](2Kgs.10.15)). To seat someone on one’s right hand denoted favor ([Pss 16:11](Ps.16.11); [77:10](Ps.77.10); [110:1](Ps.110.1)). Clean hands symbolized innocence ([Ps 26:6](Ps.26.6)), while striking hands sealed a bargain ([Prv 6:1](Prov.6.1), KJV). Lifting the hand symbolized violence ([1 Kgs 11:26](1Kgs.11.26), RSV). The hands were used in supplicatory prayer ([Ex 17:11](Exod.17.11); [Lv 9:22](Lev.9.22); [Is 1:15](Isa.1.15); [1 Tm 2:8](1Tim.2.8)) and in making vows ([Gn 14:22](Gen.14.22), KJV; [24:2](Gen.24.2)).

Other idiomatic uses of the hands expressed jeopardizing one’s life ([Jgs 12:3](Judg.12.3)), gladness ([2 Kgs 11:12](2Kgs.11.12)), generosity ([Dt 15:11](Deut.15.11)), grief ([2 Sm 13:19](2Sam.13.19)), humility ([Prv 30:32](Prov.30.32)), and undertaking a duty ([Lk 9:62](Luke.9.62)). Manual labor is an expression of man’s dignity and duty ([Eph 4:28](Eph.4.28); [1 Thes 4:11](1Thess.4.11)), the marks of which Paul was not ashamed to display ([Acts 20:34](Acts.20.34); [1 Cor 4:12](1Cor.4.12)). Ritual hand washing was obligatory for the priests before fulfilling their office ([Ex 30:19-21](Exod.30.19-Exod.30.21); [40:30-32](Exod.40.30-Exod.40.32)). The scribes and Pharisees so misapplied this that Jesus ignored ceremonial hand washing ([Mt 15:1-20](Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20); [Lk 11:38](Luke.11.38)). Pilate’s hand washing ([Mt 27:24](Matt.27.24)) disclaimed responsibility for, or professed innocence concerning, a wrong that, however, could not be done without his consent.

When Israel went out of Egypt “with an high hand” ([Ex 14:8](Exod.14.8), KJV), the reference is to the hand or help of the Lord. The hand of the Lord represented God’s resistless power ([Dt 2:15](Deut.2.15)), judgment ([Acts 13:11](Acts.13.11); [Heb 10:31](Heb.10.31)), divine inspiration ([Ez 8:1](Ezek.8.1); [37:1](Ezek.37.1)), and providential care ([Ezr 7:6](Ezra.7.6); [Jn 10:28-29](John.10.28-John.10.29)).

The laying on of hands had a profound significance and occurs frequently in the Bible. Before making a blood sacrifice, the person making the offering, not the priest, laid hands on the victim. The act signified the transference of guilt to, or self-identification with, the victim ([Lv 1:4](Lev.1.4)). Laying on of hands signified appointment to an office, as when Moses commissioned Joshua ([Nm 27:12-23](Num.27.12-Num.27.23)), the apostles made seven disciples their associates or deputies in the ministry ([Acts 6:5-6](Acts.6.5-Acts.6.6)), and Paul and Barnabas were appointed missionaries and representatives of the church in Antioch ([13:3](Acts.13.3)). By laying on of hands, a person was made an associate with the holder of an office and was admitted to the status of that office ([1 Tm 4:14](1Tim.4.14); [2 Tm 1:6](2Tim.1.6)). The act was accompanied by prayer and was, in itself, a form of prayer. As Augustine remarks: “What else is the laying on of hands but a prayer over one?”

The laying on of hands accompanied healing in the ministry of the Lord ([Mk 6:5](Mark.6.5); [Lk 4:40](Luke.4.40); [13:11-13](Luke.13.11-Luke.13.13)) and of the disciples ([Mk 16:18](Mark.16.18); [Acts 9:12, 17](Acts.9.12 Acts.9.17); [28:8](Acts.28.8)). This expressed the self-identification and sympathy of the healer with and for the sufferer, as well as reinforced the patient’s faith and God’s imparting health to him in answer to prayer.
*See also* [Right Hand](dictionary:RightHand).

Linear measure equivalent to one-sixth of a cubit or just under three inches (7.6 centimeters) in length. The fingers, up to four ([Jer 52:21](Jer.52.21)), made a handbreadth; three handbreadths made a handstretch or span ([Ex 28:16](Exod.28.16)). *See* [Weights and Measures](dictionary:WeightsandMeasures).

Female servants. They were familiar members among many households in biblical days. The handmaid cared for the women and children of a family and served as the woman’s personal attendant. She enjoyed the protection of the law ([Lv 25:6](Lev.25.6); [Dt 5:14](Deut.5.14); [15:12-15](Deut.15.12-Deut.15.15)), and as a free wife’s maid, sometimes became a concubine where there was a childless marriage ([Gn 30:3](Gen.30.3)).
*See* [Hand](dictionary:Hand).

City in Egypt included with Zoan (or Tanis) in [Isaiah 30:4](Isa.30.4) as a center of Egyptian government to which ambassadors would be sent. This indicates that it was one of the dynastic centers. It has been identified with Heracleopolis Magna, south of Memphis, the capital of northern Egypt in Roman times, and also with Heracleopolis Parva in the eastern delta region.
*See* [Criminal Law and Punishment](dictionary:CriminalLawandPunishment); [Impalement](dictionary:Impalement).
KJV spelling of Hanniel, Ulla’s son, in [1 Chronicles 7:39](1Chr.7.39). *See* [Hanniel #2](dictionary:Hanniel).
Wife of Elkanah from Ephraim’s tribe and the mother of the prophet Samuel. The childless Hannah prayed annually at Shiloh for a son, whom she vowed to dedicate to the Lord.

The Lord answered her prayer, and she called her son Samuel. When he was weaned (probably about age three), she dedicated him at Shiloh to the service of the Lord in the sanctuary. Henceforth, Samuel lived with Eli the priest and was visited by his parents on their annual pilgrimages. Hannah had three more sons and two daughters ([1 Sm 1:1–2:21](1Sam.1.1-1Sam.2.21)). Her prophetic psalm ([1 Sm 2:1-10](1Sam.2.1-1Sam.2.10)) anticipates Mary’s song of praise, the “Magnificat” ([Lk 1:46-55](Luke.1.46-Luke.1.55)).

Northern border town of Zebulun ([Jos 19:14](Josh.19.14)), mentioned in the Amarna tablets (c. 1370 BC) and in the annals of Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC). Not yet precisely located, it has been identified with Kefr ‘Anau near Rimmon and with Tell el-Bedeiwiyah, north of Nazareth.
1. Ephod’s son and leader of Manasseh’s tribe who represented his tribe in apportioning land to Israel under Moses ([Nm 34:23](Num.34.23)).
2. Ulla’s son and warrior in the tribe of Asher ([1 Chr 7:39](1Chr.7.39)).
1. Midian’s third son, and grandson of Abraham by Keturah ([Gn 25:4](Gen.25.4); [1 Chr 1:33](1Chr.1.33)).
2. Reuben’s first son ([Gn 46:9](Gen.46.9); [Ex 6:14](Exod.6.14); [1 Chr 5:3](1Chr.5.3)) and ancestor of the Hanochites ([Nm 26:5](Num.26.5)).
Descendant of Hanoch, Reuben’s firstborn son ([Nm 26:5](Num.26.5)). *See* [Hanoch #2](dictionary:Hanoch).
*See* [Feasts and Festivals of Israel](dictionary:FeastsandFestivalsofIsrael); [Judaism](dictionary:Judaism).

1. Nahash’s son and successor to the Ammonite throne. When King Nahash died, King David of Israel sent messengers to console Hanun and to express his continued friendship. But Hanun insulted David by humiliating his messengers and accusing them of spying. This action led to war and the defeat of Ammon ([2 Sm 10:1-14](2Sam.10.1-2Sam.10.14); [11:1](2Sam.11.1); [12:26-31](2Sam.12.26-2Sam.12.31); [1 Chr 19:1–20:3](1Chr.19.1-1Chr.20.3)).
2. One who helped repair Jerusalem’s Valley Gate during the time of Nehemiah ([Neh 3:13](Neh.3.13)).
3. Zalaph’s son who repaired a section of the Jerusalem wall during the time of Nehemiah ([Neh 3:30](Neh.3.30)); perhaps the same as #2 above.

Town included in the territory allotted to Issachar’s tribe for an inheritance ([Jos 19:19](Josh.19.19)). Some scholars have identified it with et-Taiyibeh, about ten miles (16 kilometers) northwest of Beth-shan.
Head of a division of priests whom David assigned to official duties in the temple ([1 Chr 24:15](1Chr.24.15)).

Place where Tiglath-pileser of Assyria exiled Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh ([1 Chr 5:26](1Chr.5.26)). A possible miscopying of [2 Kings 17:6](2Kgs.17.6) and [18:11](2Kgs.18.11) may have substituted Hara for “cities of Media.” The Greek version reads “mountains of Media,” indicating an area east of the Tigris Valley. A district rather than a single site seems to be indicated.
Twentieth wilderness encampment of the children of Israel, and the ninth from Sinai; listed between Mt Shepher and Makheloth. Its location is unknown ([Nm 33:24-25](Num.33.24-Num.33.25)).
1. Terah’s son, brother of Abraham, and the father of Lot ([Gn 11:26-31](Gen.11.26-Gen.11.31)).
2. Caleb’s son by his concubine Ephah, a member of Judah’s tribe and the father of Gazez ([1 Chr 2:46](1Chr.2.46)).
3. Shimei’s son, a member of the Gershonite division of Levi’s tribe ([1 Chr 23:9](1Chr.23.9)).

City of northern Mesopotamia, first mentioned in [Genesis 11:31](Gen.11.31) as the destination of Terah, Abraham’s father, in migrating from Ur of the Chaldees, and his home until his death. At age 75, Abraham was commanded by God to move to a land that God had for him ([Gn 12:1-4](Gen.12.1-Gen.12.4)). There were relatives who remained in Haran, however, to whom Jacob, Abraham’s grandson, fled in fear of Esau ([27:42-43](Gen.27.42-Gen.27.43)). Jacob stayed in Haran many years while serving his Uncle Laban and acquiring Leah and Rachel as wives, as well as many sheep and goats, servants, camels, and donkeys ([30:43](Gen.30.43)).

This “city of Nahor” ([Gn 11:27-29](Gen.11.27-Gen.11.29); [24:10](Gen.24.10); [27:43](Gen.27.43)) was established in the third millennium BC, and its location on a branch of the Euphrates soon made it an important commercial center. Perhaps the ancient trade route that linked Damascus, Nineveh, and Carchemish passed by Haran. Ezekiel mentions trade between Haran and Tyre ([Ez 27:23](Ezek.27.23)). Haran was an Aramean city and was famous for its worship of the lunar Sin and Nikkal. This system was an offspring of the cult found in Sumerian Ur. Sin and his consort Nikkal were revered not only here but throughout Canaan and even in Egypt. The cult persisted past NT times, its temple finally being destroyed by Mongols in the 13th century AD. It is little wonder that God commanded Abraham to leave this seat of idolatry. Modern Harran preserves the ancient cuneiform spelling of the name (cf. KJV “Charran,” [Acts 7:2, 4](Acts.7.2 Acts.7.4)).

Terms applied to several names that appear in the accounts of King David’s “mighty men.” Shammah, one of David’s mightiest men, and Jonathan’s father (a different Jonathan than Saul’s son and David’s friend) is called a Hararite ([2 Sm 23:11, 33](2Sam.23.11 2Sam.23.33); [1 Chr 11:34](1Chr.11.34) has “Shagee”), as is Agee, Shammah’s father ([2 Sm 23:11](2Sam.23.11)). Sharar, Ahiam’s father, is also so named ([2 Sm 23:33](2Sam.23.33); [1 Chr 11:35](1Chr.11.35) has “Sachar”). The meaning of the terms are uncertain; possibly “mountain” from the location of a village (Harar) or “mountaineer.”

One of King Ahasuerus’s seven personal attendants. They were ordered by Ahasuerus to parade Queen Vashti before a drunken banquet to satisfy his vanity ([Est 1:10](Esth.1.10)). Harbona later suggested that Haman be hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai ([7:9](Esth.7.9)).
A phrase signifying spiritual obstinacy.

The first references to the hardening of the heart exemplify the fundamental features of this doctrine in Scripture. The number of times it is referred to is surprising; there are at least 20 references to the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart in the OT alone, as well as Paul’s exposition of its significance in [Romans 9:17-24](Rom.9.17-Rom.9.24).

The first reference is [Exodus 4:21](Exod.4.21), where God promises Moses that he will harden Pharaoh’s heart that he might not allow the Israelites to go. This promise is repeated (see [Ex 7:3](Exod.7.3); [14:4, 17](Exod.14.4 Exod.14.17)) and rapidly comes to pass ([7:13-14](Exod.7.13-Exod.7.14)), as revelation and miracle follow one another before the eyes of Pharaoh, followed by the actual occurrence of the events God warned about, including all the judgments of the 10 plagues.

No doubt is left in the mind of the reader, either in the exodus account itself or later, that Pharaoh’s obstinacy was an act of divine judgment on God’s part for his own external ends and purposes ([Ex 9:16](Exod.9.16); [Jos 11:20](Josh.11.20); cf. [Rom 9:17-18](Rom.9.17-Rom.9.18)). Nevertheless, it is also stated that Pharaoh hardened his own heart ([Ex 8:15, 32](Exod.8.15 Exod.8.32); [9:34](Exod.9.34); [13:15](Exod.13.15)), showing that the hardening process is a deliberate product of personal rebellion against revealed truth. This is a crucial aspect of the scriptural presentation of the matter; judicial hardening of the heart is not only an act of God upon the sinner’s nature but also a willful turning from the truth. The sinner is therefore responsible to God for his hardness of heart.

The process of judicial hardening is described by Paul in [Romans 1:18-32](Rom.1.18-Rom.1.32). All humans have an innate God-consciousness from which they deliberately turn away. They change the truth into a lie and suppress what truth they have. As a result, hardness of heart takes over. Paul’s expression for this is that “their foolish heart was darkened” because “God gave them up” to the results of their own sin. The results are both intellectual (“God gave them over to a reprobate mind”) and moral, as well as social or cultural. Paul uses the term “hardness of heart” in [Romans 2:5](Rom.2.5) to describe the general result. It is important to note that it is not against God’s wrath or against the results of sin that the wicked are in revolt but against “truth” and against their own conscience ([2:14-16](Rom.2.14-Rom.2.16)).

God often warns his people not to harden their hearts, for Scripture associates hardening with unbelief ([Dt 15:7](Deut.15.7); [Heb 3:8, 15](Heb.3.8 Heb.3.15); [4:7](Heb.4.7)). Jesus was grieved at the callousness of his hearers’ hearts ([Mk 3:5](Mark.3.5); [16:14](Mark.16.14)). He referred to allowances God had made to the Jews concerning divorce because of the hardness of their hearts ([Mt 19:8](Matt.19.8)).

On at least two occasions in the Gospels, judicial blindness is ascribed directly to God, and its purpose stated ([Mt 13:13-15](Matt.13.13-Matt.13.15); [Jn 12:39-41](John.12.39-John.12.41)). Hardness of heart is therefore an aspect of the development of the fallen character, manifesting the root of rebellion ([Ps 95:8](Ps.95.8); [Jn 12:40](John.12.40); [Heb 3:8, 15](Heb.3.8 Heb.3.15); [4:7](Heb.4.7)). Throughout Scripture, Jewish apostasy is so described ([2 Kgs 17:14](2Kgs.17.14); [Neh 9:16-17](Neh.9.16-Neh.9.17); [Heb 3:8](Heb.3.8)).
*See also* [Blindness](dictionary:Blindness); [Judgment](dictionary:Judgment); [Regeneration](dictionary:Regeneration).
Small, swift, long-eared mammal similar to the rabbit ([Lv 11:6](Lev.11.6); [Dt 14:7](Deut.14.7)). *See* [Animals](dictionary:Animals).
Caleb’s descendant from Judah’s tribe and founder (or perhaps father) of Beth-gader ([1 Chr 2:51](1Chr.2.51)).
KJV spelling of Hereth in [1 Samuel 22:5](1Sam.22.5). *See* [Hereth](dictionary:Hereth).
Father of Uzziel, a goldsmith who worked to rebuild the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah’s time ([Neh 3:8](Neh.3.8)).

Shallum’s grandfather. Shallum’s wife was Huldah the prophetess ([2 Kgs 22:14](2Kgs.22.14); spelled “Hasrah” in [2 Chr 34:22](2Chr.34.22)), who delivered an oracle for Josiah after the discovery of the Book of the Law by the high priest Hilkiah.
Mountain in Aijalon of Dan’s territory ([Jgs 1:35](Judg.1.35)). *See* [Heres #1](dictionary:Heres).
Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Ezr 2:51](Ezra.2.51); [Neh 7:53](Neh.7.53)).
1. Priest whom King David appointed to official duties in the temple ([1 Chr 24:8](1Chr.24.8)).

2. Ancestor of a Jewish family who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel ([Ezr 2:32](Ezra.2.32); [Neh 10:5](Neh.10.5)). Members of this family were guilty of marrying foreign women ([Ezr 10:31](Ezra.10.31)), but they divorced their wives and a representative of the clan signed Ezra’s covenant ([Neh 10:27](Neh.10.27)).

3. Ancestor of a family of priests who returned from the exile with Zerubbabel ([Ezr 2:39](Ezra.2.39); [Neh 7:42](Neh.7.42)). Some identify him with #1 above. Members of this family were guilty of marrying foreign women.
4. Ancestor of Malkijah. Malkijah repaired a section of the Jerusalem wall during Nehemiah’s time ([Neh 3:11](Neh.3.11)). This Harim could be the same as #2 above.

5. Priest who returned from the exile with Zerubbabel ([Neh 12:3](Neh.12.3); Hebrew “Rehum,” see NLT mg). His son (or grandson) Adna is listed as a leading priest during the high priesthood of Joiakim ([12:15](Neh.12.15)). Later, under Ezra, a representative of the family (probably related to #3 above) signed the covenant of faithfulness to God ([10:5](Neh.10.5)).

Ancestor of a family who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Neh 7:24](Neh.7.24)). The name Jorah appears in the parallel list of [Ezra 2:18](Ezra.2.18). A representative of this family signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others ([Neh 10:19](Neh.10.19)).
*See* [Prostitute, Prostitution](dictionary:ProstituteProstitution).

Place mentioned by the prophet Amos to which the inhabitants of Bashan would be exiled ([Am 4:3](Amos.4.3), NLT mg). Harmon occurs only once in the Bible, and there is no known place with such a name. There are problems with the text and numerous emendations have been proposed. Some Hebrew manuscripts render it as a common noun, meaning “palace” (KJV), rather than a proper name. The Septuagint renders it “the mountain of Rimmon,” perhaps referring to a hill east of Rimmon (see [Jgs 20:45-47](Judg.20.45-Judg.20.47); cf. [Jos 15:32](Josh.15.32); [19:13](Josh.19.13)).
Zophah’s son from Asher’s tribe ([1 Chr 7:36](1Chr.7.36)).

1. Spring beside which Gideon and his army camped before their encounter with the Midianites ([Jgs 7:1](Judg.7.1)). Perhaps this is the same spring by which Saul and his army pitched their tents prior to their battle with the Philistines ([1 Sm 29:1](1Sam.29.1)). The spring of Harod is at ‘Ain Jalud by the northern side of Mt Gilboa, about two miles (3.2 kilometers) southeast of Zerin.

2. Home of Shammah and Elika, two of David’s valiant warriors ([2 Sm 23:25](2Sam.23.25)). In the parallel passage ([1 Chr 11:27](1Chr.11.27)), Elika’s name is omitted and Shammah (Shammoth) is listed as a Harorite instead of a Harodite. “Harorite” reflects a later scribal error where the copyist mistook the Hebrew letter “d” for an “r.”
Designation for Shammah and Elika, two of David’s mighty men ([2 Sm 23:25](2Sam.23.25)). *See* [Harod #2](dictionary:Harod).
Alternate name of Reaiah, Shobal’s son, in [1 Chronicles 2:52](1Chr.2.52). *See* [Reaiah #1](dictionary:Reaiah).
Alternate description of one of David’s mighty men ([1 Chr 11:27](1Chr.11.27)). *See* [Harod #2](dictionary:Harod).

Town in Canaan that was the home of Sisera. This Canaanite general led his forces from Harosheth against Deborah and Barak ([Jgs 4:2-13](Judg.4.2-Judg.4.13), KJV “Harosheth of the Gentiles”). After his soldiers panicked, they fled back to Harosheth where they were defeated (v [16](Judg.4.16)).
Stringed instrument. *See* [Musical Instruments (Nebel)](dictionary:MusicalInstruments).

Agricultural term for implement or procedure, though no implement corresponding to the modern harrow is known from Palestine or Egypt. [Job 39:10](Job.39.10) speaks of an ox performing the harrowing, while [Isaiah 28:24](Isa.28.24) notes that plowed ground was leveled as part of the process. Like the foregoing references, [Hosea 10:11](Hos.10.11) speaks of harrowing in connection with plowing. Most probably harrowing consisted of branches being pulled behind an animal or plow to smooth the land and before seeding. *See* [Agriculture](dictionary:Agriculture).
Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Ezr 2:52](Ezra.2.52); [Neh 7:54](Neh.7.54)).
Adult male red deer. *See* [Animals (Deer)](dictionary:Animals).
Aharhel’s father from Judah’s tribe ([1 Chr 4:8](1Chr.4.8)).
Jedaiah’s father. Jedaiah helped repair the wall of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah ([Neh 3:10](Neh.3.10)).
Name applied to Shephatiah, one of David’s ambidextrous warriors from Benjamin’s tribe who joined him at Ziklag ([1 Chr 12:5](1Chr.12.5)). Whether the name refers to a family or a place is uncertain.
Maternal grandfather of Amon, king of Judah ([2 Kgs 21:19](2Kgs.21.19)).

The gathering in of a crop, especially for food. There was no single harvesttime in ancient Israel. Olives were harvested in September–November, flax in March– April, barley in April–May, and wheat in May–June. Fruits such as figs and grapes were harvested at the end of the summer, in August or September. The Israelites’ calendar revolved around the harvest periods (cf. [Jgs 15:1](Judg.15.1); [Ru 1:22](Ruth.1.22)).

In the OT, Pentecost (a harvest festival) was one of the three major festivals that the Israelites were required by the Lord to keep annually ([Ex 23:16](Exod.23.16)). In doing so they would remember that the rich land into which they had been brought from Egypt ([Dt 8:7-10](Deut.8.7-Deut.8.10)) was the gift of God. In offering the firstfruits of the harvest ([Lv 23:10-11](Lev.23.10-Lev.23.11)), the Israelites showed gratitude and acknowledged their dependence on the Lord. Moreover, as the harvest was a gift, they were not to be selfish in enjoying it but to leave some for the underprivileged ([19:9-10](Lev.19.9-Lev.19.10); [23:22](Lev.23.22)).

NT references to harvest are largely figurative. In one parable ([Mt 13:24-30](Matt.13.24-Matt.13.30)) harvest represents the final judgment and the reapers are angels, gathering in the righteous and excluding the wicked from the kingdom (vv [36-43](Matt.13.36-Matt.13.43)). In another, the harvest refers to those who have not yet heard the gospel, and the “laborers” are those who bring it to them ([Mt 9:37-38](Matt.9.37-Matt.9.38)).
*See also* [Agriculture](dictionary:Agriculture); [Feasts and Festivals of Israel](dictionary:FeastsandFestivalsofIsrael); [Vines, Vineyard](dictionary:VinesVineyard).
One of Zerubbabel’s sons ([1 Chr 3:20](1Chr.3.20)).
KJV rendering of Hassenuah in [1 Chronicles 9:7](1Chr.9.7). *See* [Hassenuah](dictionary:Hassenuah).
1. Ancestor of Ethan, a Levite and descendant of Merari. Ethan was a musician in the temple during the reign of David ([1 Chr 6:45](1Chr.6.45)).
2. Ancestor of a group of Levites who helped rebuild the temple after the Babylonian exile ([1 Chr 9:14](1Chr.9.14); [Neh 11:15](Neh.11.15)).
3. Jeduthun’s son, a Levite and musician in the temple during the time of David ([1 Chr 25:3, 19](1Chr.25.3 1Chr.25.19)).
4. Head of a group of Hebronites who was given the position of overseer of Israel west of the Jordan. He was in charge of both political and religious activities ([1 Chr 26:30](1Chr.26.30)).
5. Kemuel’s son, a Levite and head of a household during the reign of David ([1 Chr 27:17](1Chr.27.17)).
6. Chief of the Levites who participated in the Passover kept by King Josiah in the kingdom of Judah (640–609 BC; [2 Chr 35:9](2Chr.35.9)).
7. Merarite Levite who returned to Jerusalem from Babylon with Ezra ([Ezr 8:19](Ezra.8.19)).
8. Priest who returned to Jerusalem from Babylon with Ezra ([Ezr 8:24](Ezra.8.24)); perhaps the same person as #7 above.
9. Parosh’s son, who obeyed Ezra’s exhortation to divorce his pagan wife after the exile ([Ezr 10:25](Ezra.10.25)); possibly the same as Asibias (1 Esd 9:26).

10. Ruler over half the district of Keilah (a city of Judah in the Shephelah district of Libnah-mareshah) who participated in rebuilding the Jerusalem wall for his district after the exile ([Neh 3:17](Neh.3.17)).
11. Levite who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God ([Neh 10:11](Neh.10.11)).
12. Ancestor of Uzzi, an overseer of Levites in Jerusalem after the exile ([Neh 11:22](Neh.11.22)).
13. Priest and head of a household in Palestine after the exile during the time of the high priest Joiakim ([Neh 12:21](Neh.12.21)).
14. Chief of the Levites and a temple musician after the exile during the time of Joiakim the high priest ([Neh 12:24](Neh.12.24)); perhaps the same person as #11 above.
One of the leaders who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile ([Neh 10:25](Neh.10.25)).
1. Hattush’s father. Hattush assisted in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem during Nehemiah’s day ([Neh 3:10](Neh.3.10)).
2. Levite who joined with others in an invocation at the covenant-signing ceremony ([Neh 9:5](Neh.9.5)).
Man, possibly of Levite origin, who stood on Ezra’s left when Ezra read the law to the people ([Neh 8:4](Neh.8.4)).
Warrior among David’s mighty men ([1 Chr 11:34](1Chr.11.34), NLT mg); alternately called Jashen in [2 Samuel 23:32](2Sam.23.32). *See* [Jashen](dictionary:Jashen).

One of the places where the Israelites stopped during the 40 years they wandered in the wilderness ([Nm 33:29-30](Num.33.29-Num.33.30)). *See* [Wilderness Wanderings](dictionary:WildernessWanderings).
KJV alternate spelling of Hasshub. *See* [Hasshub](dictionary:Hasshub).
One of Zerubbabel’s sons ([1 Chr 3:20](1Chr.3.20)).
1. Ancestor of a family who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Ezr 2:19](Ezra.2.19); [10:33](Ezra.10.33); [Neh 7:22](Neh.7.22)).
2. Israelite who stood to Ezra’s left at the reading of the law ([Neh 8:4](Neh.8.4)).
3. Leader who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile ([Neh 10:18](Neh.10.18)).
KJV alternate spelling of Hasupha in [Nehemiah 7:46](Neh.7.46). *See* [Hasupha](dictionary:Hasupha).

Transliterations of a Hebrew word meaning “the pious.” The influence of Greek customs and ways threatened the preservation of Jewish patterns of life in the third and fourth centuries BC. Jews were required to employ the Greek language in their daily lives, and with the language came the influence of Greek culture. This process was quite apparent in Palestine during the second century BC, and the Jewish people responded in two antagonistic ways: one party was friendly to the Greeks; the other party set as their goal strict adherence to the principles of Judaism. The latter group, known as “the pious,” or Hasideans, cherished the ideals of responsible covenant observance ([Dt 7:9](Deut.7.9)), and in the Maccabean period became militants in their efforts to worship God according to the Mosaic law. Both the Pharisees and the Essenes may have had early roots in the Hasidim movement.
*See also* [Essenes](dictionary:Essenes); [Judaism](dictionary:Judaism); [Pharisees](dictionary:Pharisees).
Family name of the Jews who instigated the Jewish revolt against the Greeks in 167 BC. *See* [Judaism](dictionary:Judaism).
Variant spelling of Harhas, Shallum’s grandfather, in [2 Chronicles 34:22](2Chr.34.22) (NLT mg). *See* [Harhas](dictionary:Harhas).
Alternate name for Senaah in [Nehemiah 3:3](Neh.3.3). *See* [Senaah](dictionary:Senaah).

Ancestor of a Benjamite family that returned to Judah with Zerubbabel after the exile ([1 Chr 9:7](1Chr.9.7); [Neh 11:9](Neh.11.9), KJV “Senuah”); perhaps alternately called Senaah ([Ezr 2:35](Ezra.2.35); [Neh 7:38](Neh.7.38)), and Hassenaah ([Neh 3:3](Neh.3.3)). *See* [Senaah](dictionary:Senaah).
1. Merari clan leader of Levi’s tribe. Hasshub was the father of Shemaiah, a settler in Jerusalem after the return from captivity ([1 Chr 9:14](1Chr.9.14); [Neh 11:15](Neh.11.15)).
2. Pahath-moab’s son, who repaired a section of the Jerusalem wall and the Tower of the Ovens during the time of Nehemiah ([Neh 3:11](Neh.3.11)).
3. Another Hasshub who repaired the Jerusalem wall opposite his house ([Neh 3:23](Neh.3.23)).
4. Leader who signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God with Nehemiah and others after the exile ([Neh 10:23](Neh.10.23)).

Ancestor of a family of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Ezr 2:55](Ezra.2.55), NLT mg). He is perhaps identifiable with Sophereth in [Nehemiah 7:57](Neh.7.57).

Ancestor of a group of temple assistants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Ezr 2:43](Ezra.2.43); [Neh 7:46](Neh.7.46)). He is perhaps the same person as Gishpa in [Nehemiah 11:21](Neh.11.21). *See* [Gishpa, Gispa](dictionary:GishpaGispa).
*See* [Head Covering](dictionary:HeadCovering).

Eunuch appointed by the Persian king Ahasuerus to wait on Esther. Hathach brought Esther messages from Mordecai. In this way Esther learned of Haman’s plot against the Jews ([Est 4:5-10](Esth.4.5-Esth.4.10)).
Othniel’s son and the grandson of Kenaz ([1 Chr 4:13](1Chr.4.13)).
Ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the captivity ([Ezr 2:54](Ezra.2.54); [Neh 7:56](Neh.7.56)).
Ancestor of a family of gatekeepers who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Ezr 2:42](Ezra.2.42); [Neh 7:45](Neh.7.45)).

Intense feeling of aversion or enmity, which could prompt a person to loathe someone or something, or even to seek revenge for having been wronged. The Scriptures forbid people to hate others ([Lv 19:17-18](Lev.19.17-Lev.19.18)) because it leads to sin. Indeed, hatred itself is considered murder ([1 Jn 3:15](1John.3.15)). We are called upon to let God, the holy one, avenge all wrongs ([Prv 20:22](Prov.20.22)), and we are commanded by Jesus to love our enemies ([Mt 5:43-44](Matt.5.43-Matt.5.44)).

Not all aspects of hatred are sinful. The Scriptures tell us that God hates evil ([Prv 6:16-19](Prov.6.16-Prov.6.19)) and evil people ([Ps 5:5](Ps.5.5)). The Scripture also has expressions such as “Jacob have I loved; Esau I have hated” ([Mal 1:2-3](Mal.1.2-Mal.1.3)). This means that God elected Jacob and not Esau to be the progenitor of the chosen Jewish race. In similar fashion, would-be Christians are challenged by Jesus to hate their lives and earthly relationships if they want to follow him ([Lk 14:26](Luke.14.26)). This means that they must choose Jesus above all else.
Forefather of a family of King Soloman’s servants who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the exile ([Ezr 2:57](Ezra.2.57); [Neh 7:59](Neh.7.59)).
1. Shemaiah’s son and a descendant of David ([1 Chr 3:22](1Chr.3.22)). Hattush returned from the Babylonian exile with Ezra ([Ezr 8:3](Ezra.8.3)).
2. Son of Hashabneiah, who helped Nehemiah rebuild the walls of Jerusalem ([Neh 3:10](Neh.3.10)).

3. Priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel ([Neh 12:2](Neh.12.2)). One of his descendants signed Ezra’s covenant of faithfulness to God ([Neh 10:4](Neh.10.4)). His name is omitted from [Nehemiah 12:14](Neh.12.14) through scribal error.

Region in northeastern Transjordan mentioned in Ezekiel’s description of the borders of the land ([Ez 47:16-18](Ezek.47.16-Ezek.47.18)). In biblical times it corresponded to the modern Jebel ed-Druze of the Leja. This area is mentioned as early as the reign of Shalmaneser III of Assyria in his description of a military campaign in 841 BC. His army marched to Mt Khauranu after a siege of Damascus and before crossing Galilee to Mt Carmel.

In 733–732 BC Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria conquered Damascus and its surrounding region and organized it into provinces, one of which was Khaurina, or Hauran. The same province is mentioned in the Annals of Ashurbanipal during his campaign against the Arabians (639–637 BC).
1. Descendant of Cush ([Gn 10:7](Gen.10.7); [1 Chr 1:9](1Chr.1.9)).
2. Descendant of Shem through Joktan ([Gn 10:29](Gen.10.29); [1 Chr 1:23](1Chr.1.23)).

Land in the neighborhood of Eden, now unknown but said to be watered by the river Pishon and containing supplies of gold, bdellium, and onyx stone ([Gn 2:11-12](Gen.2.11-Gen.2.12)). The location of Havilah has been a matter of much dispute. It cannot have any connection with the Havilah of [1 Samuel 15:7](1Sam.15.7), where Saul fought against certain Amalekites, because the locale of the Eden narratives is Mesopotamian and not Palestinian. On the same basis, any attempt to locate Havilah in southern Arabia, Somaliland, or India would be mistaken. The “river” Pishon may have been an irrigation canal, since Akkadian does not have a separate word for these two different bodies of water, and the Mesopotamian custom was to name large irrigation canals as if they were rivers. This would help to account for the survival of the name “Pishon” long after the canal had disappeared. The Pishon was one of four branches that the river formed once it left Eden; hence, Havilah must have been to the north, since the narrative assumes an upstream perspective. Probably Havilah was in the general area of the Shinar plain and was watered by a major irrigation canal. Both Havilah and the canal have long disappeared.

Series of settlements on the edge of Bashan across the Jordan captured by Jair, according to [Numbers 32:41](Num.32.41) (NLT mg). Because of their location, they fell into the allotment of the half-tribe of Manasseh. The number of these villages is given in [Joshua 13:29-30](Josh.13.29-Josh.13.30) as 60, and they are probably included in the cities and towns of [1 Chronicles 2:22-23](1Chr.2.22-1Chr.2.23), although only 23 cities are specified as belonging to Jair. The KJV rendering as “Bashan-havoth-jair” ([Dt 3:14](Deut.3.14)) makes the location as specific as in the Hebrew. In [Judges 10:4](Judg.10.4), a judge named Jair had 30 sons who controlled 30 cities named Havvoth-jair. But he is obviously different from the Jair of [Numbers 32:41](Num.32.41). If his sons controlled only 30 settlements, he himself probably governed the remaining 30. In [1 Chronicles 2:21-24](1Chr.2.21-1Chr.2.24), which reflects a relationship between Judah and Manasseh, Jair was said to have 23 cities in Gilead when Geshur and Aram captured 60 towns from the tent settlements of Jair and Kenath and its dependencies. While the variant numbers present difficulties, the narrative itself may be the Chronicler’s way of indicating Judah’s sense of sovereignty over Gilead.
*See* [Birds](dictionary:Birds).
Dried grass used as animal fodder.

King of Syria (843?–796? BC) who came to power by assassinating his ruler, Ben-hadad ([2 Kgs 8:7-15](2Kgs.8.7-2Kgs.8.15)), and establishing a new dynasty. An inscription of Shalmaneser speaks of Hazael as a “son of a nobody,” and mentions that he had “seized the throne.” The Hebrew prophet Elijah was told to anoint Hazael as the next king of Syria ([1 Kgs 19:15](1Kgs.19.15)).

Upon becoming king, Hazael continued the policy of Ben-hadad in resisting the Assyrian military influence in Palestine. Although most of Palestine came under Assyrian control in 841 BC, Hazael was able to retain independence by withstanding the siege of Damascus. Failing in a final attempt to subdue Damascus in 837 BC, the Assyrians withdrew. This allowed Hazael the freedom to begin a series of attacks against Israel that resulted in Syrian domination of most of Palestine.

Toward the end of Jehu’s reign in Israel, Hazael occupied Israelite territory in the hills of Galilee and east of the Jordan ([2 Kgs 10:32](2Kgs.10.32)). After Jehu’s death, the Syrian king continually harassed Israel, captured much of Philistia, and spared Jerusalem only because Joash, king of Judah, asked for peace and was willing to pay heavy tribute ([12:17-18](2Kgs.12.17-2Kgs.12.18)). The Syrian oppression continued during the reign of Hazael’s son until Adad-nirari III, king of Assyria, marched into Syria, causing Damascus to submit and pay heavy tribute. This took the pressure off Israel and provided opportunity for her to regain territory taken by Hazael ([13:24-25](2Kgs.13.24-2Kgs.13.25)).

Archaeologists found the remains of a bed at Arslan Tash (Hadathah) that may have been included in the tribute taken from Damascus. Part of the inscription on a piece of ivory inlay from the bed reads “to our Lord Hazael.” Evidently there was a high level of culture in Damascus under Hazael. According to Josephus, Hazael was long remembered for his part in building temples in Damascus.
*See also* [Syria, Syrians](dictionary:SyriaSyrians).
Maaseiah’s descendant from Judah’s tribe, who was one of the leaders in Jerusalem after the exile ([Neh 11:5](Neh.11.5)).

Town that, with Azmon, defined the southern border of Judah ([Nm 34:4](Num.34.4)), usually identified with Khirbet el-Qudeirat near Kadesh-barnea. The parallel passage in [Joshua 15:3-4](Josh.15.3-Josh.15.4) lists four places—Hezron, Addar, Karka, and Azmon—instead of two. Some have suggested that Hazar-addar and Addar are the same place; others, that it was renamed Hezron to distinguish it from Addar.

Place describing the northeast corner of Israel’s border ([Nm 34:9-10](Num.34.9-Num.34.10)); alternately spelled Hazar-enon in [Ezekiel 47:17-18](Ezek.47.17-Ezek.47.18) and [48:1](Ezek.48.1) (RSV). It is identified with modern Hadr at the base of Mt Hermon.
City in the southern extremity of the land assigned to Judah’s tribe for an inheritance ([Jos 15:27](Josh.15.27)).
KJV spelling of the place Hazer-hatticon in [Ezekiel 47:16](Ezek.47.16). *See* [Hazer-hatticon](dictionary:HazerHatticon).

Descendant of Shem through Joktan ([Gn 10:26](Gen.10.26); [1 Chr 1:20](1Chr.1.20)) whose progeny lived in southern Arabia ([Gn 10:30](Gen.10.30)) in the Wadi Hadhramaut. Excavations there revealed a flourishing economy in the fifth century BC, based on frankincense trade. This trade, revived in the second century BC, made the area prosperous and influential.

Simeonite city located in the southern section of Judah ([Jos 15:28](Josh.15.28); [19:3](Josh.19.3); [1 Chr 4:28](1Chr.4.28)). It is also listed among those cities occupied by the Jews who returned from captivity ([Neh 11:27](Neh.11.27)).

City assigned to Simeon within the territory allotted to Judah for an inheritance ([Jos 19:5](Josh.19.5)); alternately called Hazar-susim ([1 Chr 4:31](1Chr.4.31)). Solomon probably used it as a transfer point for horses brought from Egypt for sale to the Hittites and Syrians, as suggested by its name, meaning “horse station.” Hazar-susah has been identified with Sbalat Abu Susein, east of the Wadi Far’ah.

City identifiable with En-gedi in [2 Chronicles 20:2](2Chr.20.2). During the time of Abraham, it was inhabited by Amorites who were subdued by Kedorlaomer as he and other eastern kings swept through the area ([Gn 14:7](Gen.14.7)). It has been suggested that it may be the Tamar that Solomon fortified ([1 Kgs 9:18](1Kgs.9.18)), placed by Ezekiel southeast of Israel ([Ez 47:18-19](Ezek.47.18-Ezek.47.19); [48:28](Ezek.48.28)). Wadi Hasasa has apparently been named after the ancient site.
KJV mistranslation for almond in [Genesis 30:37](Gen.30.37). *See* [Plants (Almond)](dictionary:Plants).
KJV spelling of Hazzelelponi, Etam’s daughter, in [1 Chronicles 4:3](1Chr.4.3). *See* [Hazzelelponi](dictionary:Hazzelelponi).

Boundary marker along Israel’s northern perimeter ([Ez 47:16](Ezek.47.16)). In conjunction with the use of Hazar-enan in this context, and in comparison with [Numbers 34:9-10](Num.34.9-Num.34.10), it appears that Hazer-hatticon may represent a scribal error for Hazar-enan.
KJV transliteration of the corresponding Hebrew word in [Deuteronomy 2:23](Deut.2.23). Instead of the proper name for a city, it may be a generic term for “villages,” a rendering favored by the NLT.

Camp of the Israelites during their wanderings in the desert. It was the third camp from Mt Sinai ([Nm 11:35](Num.11.35); [12:16](Num.12.16); [33:17-18](Num.33.17-Num.33.18); [Dt 1:1](Deut.1.1)). Here Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses for marrying a Cushite woman and questioned whether God spoke only through Moses ([Nm 12:1-2](Num.12.1-Num.12.2)). The site is probably modern ‘Ain Khadra, about 30 miles (48 kilometers) northeast of Jebel Musa.
*See also* [Wilderness Wanderings](dictionary:WildernessWanderings).
KJV spelling of the city Hazazon-tamar in [Genesis 14:7](Gen.14.7). *See* [Hazazon-tamar](dictionary:HazazonTamar).
Levite and son of Shimei during David’s time ([1 Chr 23:9](1Chr.23.9)).

Nahor’s fifth son ([Gn 22:22](Gen.22.22)); probably used as the name for a Nahorite clan. It has been identified with the name Hazu, which designated a mountainous region in northern Arabia mentioned in an inscription telling of Esarhaddon’s Arabian campaign.

1. City in northern Palestine in the territory of Naphtali, called “the capital of the federation of all these kingdoms \[of Canaan\]” in [Joshua 11:10](Josh.11.10). Located five miles (8 kilometers) southwest of Lake Huleh and ten miles (16 kilometers) north of the Sea of Galilee, it is known as Tell el-Qedah (or Tell Waggas) today. At its peak it numbered 40,000 inhabitants and was by far the largest Canaanite city in area and population. It was a great commercial center on the trade routes between Egypt and Babylon.

Hazor is first mentioned in the 19th-century BC Egyptian Execration Texts. It is given prominence in the archives of Mari (18th century BC), being the only Palestinian city to be mentioned in these documents. It is frequently mentioned in Egyptian documents from the time of Thutmose III to Ramses II, including the Tell el-Amarna correspondence.

The OT mentions Hazor a number of times. The first time concerns the conquests of Joshua in which Hazor was completely destroyed ([Jos 11:1-15](Josh.11.1-Josh.11.15); [12:19](Josh.12.19)). At that time, Hazor was a Canaanite royal city whose king, Jabin, headed a northern Canaanite federation against the invading Israelites. Hazor figures in the revolt led by Deborah and Barak against another Jabin that resulted in a rout of Jabin’s forces under Sisera ([Jgs 4–5](Judg.4.1-Judg.5.31)). Hazor was fortified by Solomon ([1 Kgs 9:15](1Kgs.9.15)); the remains of Solomon’s Hazor are clearly preserved. King Ahab (874–853 BC) also added to the fortifications; the elaborate water system Ahab constructed when he rebuilt the whole upper city and fortified it to withstand long siege has been found. The city was destroyed by the Assyrian Tiglath-pileser III about 732 BC, thus bringing to an end its use as a fortified Israelite city ([2 Kgs 15:29](2Kgs.15.29)). Fortresses of the Assyrian, Persian, and Hellenistic periods have been found in various strata of the city. Hazor is not mentioned again in the OT, but 1 Maccabees 11:67 says Jonathan encamped near the plain of Hazor where he fought against Demetrius (147 BC). The last mention of Hazor in ancient sources was by Josephus.

Hazor has been of particular interest for the light it sheds on the conquest of Palestine described in Joshua. Excavations clearly show that the great city was destroyed by fire in the last half of the 13th century BC and was never rebuilt. Archaeological finds support the biblical picture of a violent conquest under Joshua. The meager Israelite occupation in the 12th and 11th century BC was replaced by a well-fortified city during the Solomonic era.
2. Town in southern Judah ([Jos 15:23](Josh.15.23)). It is perhaps el-Jebariyeh, on the Wadi Umm Ethnan near Bir Hafir, about nine miles (14.5 kilometers) southeast of el-’Auja.
3. Another town in southern Judah, called Hazor-hadattah ([Jos 15:25](Josh.15.25)). The KJV translates as separate cities, “Hazor, Hadattah.” *See* [Hazor-hadattah](dictionary:HazorHadattah).

4. Alternate name for Kerioth-hezron ([Jos 15:25](Josh.15.25)), probably situated in southern Judah. The KJV translates as separate cities, “Kerioth, and Hezron.” *See* [Kerioth #1](dictionary:Kerioth).
5. Town north of Jerusalem occupied by Benjamites after their return from exile ([Neh 11:33](Neh.11.33)). The name has been preserved in modern Khirbet Hazzur, west of Beit Hanina.
6. Place somewhere in the Arabian Desert east of Palestine. Jeremiah refers to its kingdoms in his oracle of judgment against Kedar and Hazor ([Jer 49:28-33](Jer.49.28-Jer.49.33)).

One of the cities located in the southern extremity of Judah, near the border of Edom ([Jos 15:25](Josh.15.25)). The KJV translates the term as two different cities, “Hazor and Hadattah.” The Aramaic adjective “Hadattah” indicates this as a settlement from Hazor, but this is unsure.
Etam’s daughter from Judah’s tribe ([1 Chr 4:3](1Chr.4.3)).

The uppermost portion of the body, containing the brain, major sense organs, and the mouth. It appears many times in the Bible as a physical description. The Hebrew term for *head* is also used figuratively in the Old Testament. Frequently, it designates prominence or authority.

To raise one’s head was considered an act of pride ([Ps 140:9](Ps.140.9)) or honor ([Gn 40:20](Gen.40.20); [Pss 3:3](Ps.3.3); [27:6](Ps.27.6)). Bowing the head signified humility ([Is 58:5](Isa.58.5)) or sadness ([Lam 2:10](Lam.2.10)). The Hebrew word is used metaphorically of mountain peaks ([Gn 8:5](Gen.8.5)), the tops of buildings ([Gn 11:4](Gen.11.4)) or trees ([2 Sm 5:24](2Sam.5.24)), and river sources ([Gn 2:10](Gen.2.10)). The term was commonly used to designate positions of political, military, or familiar authority. In this sense the “head” exercised control over all those subjected to him ([Jgs 10:18](Judg.10.18); [1 Sm 15:17](1Sam.15.17); [Ps 18:43](Ps.18.43); [Is 7:8-9](Isa.7.8-Isa.7.9); [Jer 31:7](Jer.31.7); [Hos 1:11](Hos.1.11)). David was called the “keeper of mine head” (KJV) when he served as the bodyguard of Achish ([1 Sm 28:2](1Sam.28.2); cf. [Jgs 9:53](Judg.9.53); [Ps 68:21](Ps.68.21)).

Greek philosophers used the image of the body to represent the universe. The head of this body—called Zeus or Reason—was considered responsible for the creation and sustenance of the remaining members (celestial beings, humans, animals, plants, and inanimate objects). The universe, or “body,” owed its existence to the “head.”

Between 460 BC (the date usually ascribed to the first writings of Hippocrates) and AD 200 (the death of Galen, who developed Hippocrates’ findings), Greek medical science came to understand the head as the seat of intelligence. The body was able to operate efficiently only because the brain was capable of interpreting data received from the body (eyes, ears, skin, and so on), and because it was able to send out appropriate impulses to the various members of the body, based upon the data received. The ability of the brain to interpret and direct made the existence of the body completely dependent upon it.

In the NT, the term refers to the actual human head ([Mt 5:36](Matt.5.36); [6:17](Matt.6.17); [14:8](Matt.14.8); [26:7](Matt.26.7); [Mk 6:27](Mark.6.27); [14:3](Mark.14.3); [Lk 7:46](Luke.7.46); [Jn 13:9](John.13.9); [20:7](John.20.7)), to apocalyptic beings ([Rv 1:14](Rev.1.14); [4:4](Rev.4.4); [12:1](Rev.12.1)), and to animals ([Rv 9:7, 17, 19](Rev.9.7 Rev.9.17 Rev.9.19); [12:3](Rev.12.3)). Furthermore, it appears in such expressions as “to heap coals of fire upon the head,” meaning to return good for evil ([Rom 12:20](Rom.12.20); cf. [Mt 5:44](Matt.5.44)); to “shear” or “anoint the head” expressing a vow ([Acts 21:24](Acts.21.24)); and “to lay down the head,” meaning to sleep ([Mt 8:20](Matt.8.20); [Lk 9:58](Luke.9.58)).

The apostle Paul drew from the OT metaphorical understanding of the term to express the headship of God over Christ, Christ over man, and man over woman ([1 Cor 11:3-16](1Cor.11.3-1Cor.11.16); cf. [Eph 5:23](Eph.5.23)). In the light of these relationships, Paul encouraged women at Corinth to wear veils in worship. The veil gave a woman the authority to worship as an equal with men before God. The term is used again with the meaning “authority” to express the lordship of Christ over the universe ([Eph 1:21-22](Eph.1.21-Eph.1.22); [Col 2:10](Col.2.10)).

Paul used the image of the head and body to express the relationship between Christ and his church ([Eph 4:15](Eph.4.15); [5:23](Eph.5.23); cf. [1 Cor 12:12-27](1Cor.12.12-1Cor.12.27)). In addition to the OT sense, the contributions of medical science in Paul’s day may provide insight into this image, for Christ is not only the dominant ruler over the church but also the dynamic force that provides its direction and unity. The ability of the church to exist and the focal point of its activity are rooted in the work of its “head,” Jesus Christ. In this light, various modern exegetes have argued that headship does not mean “authority” as much as it means “source,” as in the term “fountainhead.” Thus, he who is the head is the source, the supplier. These interpreters see God as being Christ’s supplier, and Christ being the church’s supplier, and man being woman’s supplier.
Something used to cover one’s head either for protection or for religious reasons.

Men wore a cap, turban, or head scarf for protection against the sun. The cap was similar to a skullcap (a cap without a brim) and was sometimes worn by the poor. The turban ([Is 3:23](Isa.3.23)) was made of thick linen wound around the head with the ends tucked inside the folds. The priest’s turban had a plate strapped to it bearing the inscription “Holy to the LORD” ([Ex 28:36](Exod.28.36)). The head scarf was made from a square yard (.8 square meter) of cloth, folded in half to form a triangle. The sides fell over the shoulders and the V-point down the back, and it was held in place by a headband made of cord. About the second century BC, male Jews began to wear phylacteries on their foreheads, small leather boxes containing special Scripture passages, at morning prayers and at festivals, but not on the Sabbath.

Women were often veiled in public, although this custom changed over the centuries. In NT times, women usually wore veils ([1 Cor 11:5-6](1Cor.11.5-1Cor.11.6)). Women also wore a cloth similar to the head scarf, but the fabric was different in quality and color from that worn by men. It was often pinned over a stiff hat and set with ornaments. If a woman was married, these and other important coins covered the front of the hat and constituted her dowry (cf. [Lk 15:8-10](Luke.15.8-Luke.15.10)). Women also adorned their heads with an elaborate plaiting of their hair, prompting Peter to warn Christian women about too much concern with external beauty ([1 Pt 3:3-4](1Pet.3.3-1Pet.3.4)).

To make well. The OT provides the proper background for a Christian understanding of the concept of healing. In the OT the basic point is made that God is the healer of his people. In [Exodus 15:22-26](Exod.15.22-Exod.15.26), after God has delivered his people from Egypt, led them through the sea, and sweetened the water at Marah, he speaks of himself as their “healer.” This refers primarily to physical sustenance, but it points to the more encompassing concept of God sustaining his people in an eternal relationship with himself. In a similar manner, [Deuteronomy 32:39](Deut.32.39) speaks of God as the one who heals. The context in Deuteronomy implies that this healing power derives from the fact that God is God. This concept of God as the healer is echoed throughout the OT by the psalmists ([Pss 6:2](Ps.6.2); [41:4](Ps.41.4); [103:3](Ps.103.3)) and prophets ([Is 19:22](Isa.19.22); [Jer 17:14](Jer.17.14); [Hos 7:1](Hos.7.1); [Zec 11:16](Zech.11.16)).
Jesus the Healer: Accounts in the Gospels

The NT significantly emphasizes Jesus as the healer. Mark portrays him as a teacher and healer in his opening account of Jesus’ ministry in Capernaum with the healing of the demoniac, Peter’s mother-in-law, the sick brought to him in the evening, and the leper ([Mk 1:21-45](Mark.1.21-Mark.1.45)). Indeed, healing sickness and casting out demons characterize Jesus’ ministry. Mark presents in rapid succession Jesus’ healing of the paralytic ([2:1-12](Mark.2.1-Mark.2.12)), the man with the withered hand ([3:1-6](Mark.3.1-Mark.3.6)), the multitudes by the sea (vv [7-12](Mark.3.7-Mark.3.12)), the Gerasene demoniac ([5:1-20](Mark.5.1-Mark.5.20)), the woman with a hemorrhage, and Jairus’s daughter (vv [21-43](Mark.5.21-Mark.5.43)). Jesus then commissioned the Twelve to proclaim repentance, to cast out demons, and to heal the sick ([6:7-13](Mark.6.7-Mark.6.13)). He himself continued with healings at Gennesaret (vv [53-56](Mark.6.53-Mark.6.56)), casting out the unclean spirit from the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman ([7:24-30](Mark.7.24-Mark.7.30)), healing the deaf and mute man (vv [31-37](Mark.7.31-Mark.7.37)), the blind man of Bethsaida ([8:22-26](Mark.8.22-Mark.8.26)), the boy possessed with an evil spirit ([9:14-20](Mark.9.14-Mark.9.20)), and blind Bartimaeus ([10:46-52](Mark.10.46-Mark.10.52)).

Certainly healing is an important aspect of Jesus’ ministry. The healings expressed not only his compassion for those suffering but also constituted a revelation of his person. This is brought out by the climactic statement of Jesus in healing the paralytic: “that you may know that the Son of man has authority on earth to forgive sins” ([Mk 2:10](Mark.2.10), RSV). It also seems that Mark intended his readers to understand that the healing of the deaf and mute man ([7:31-37](Mark.7.31-Mark.7.37)) and the blind man of Bethsaida ([8:22-26](Mark.8.22-Mark.8.26)) symbolize the awakening of spiritual understanding in the disciples of who Jesus is. It is also significant that Mark has placed the healing of Bartimaeus ([10:46-52](Mark.10.46-Mark.10.52)) immediately after Jesus’ third announcement of his own coming death (vv [32-34](Mark.10.32-Mark.10.34)) and the disciples’ third failure to understand that his being the Messiah entailed the necessity of suffering (vv [35-45](Mark.10.35-Mark.10.45)).

Matthew also portrays Jesus as teaching, preaching, and healing ([Mt 4:23-25](Matt.4.23-Matt.4.25)), and parallels the accounts in Mark, except for the healing of the demoniac in the synagogue ([Mk 1:23-28](Mark.1.23-Mark.1.28)) and the blind man of Bethsaida ([8:22-26](Mark.8.22-Mark.8.26)). However, according to his special purpose and structure, Matthew has placed many of Jesus’ healings together in a “mighty works” section ([Mt 8–9](Matt.8.1-Matt.9.38)), complementing the “great words” (“sermon”) section (chs [5–7](Matt.5.1-Matt.7.29)). Matthew views Jesus’ healings as directly fulfilling the OT, as he states in [8:17](Matt.8.17). The unique way in which the healings of [8:16](Matt.8.16) are spoken of as fulfilling [Isaiah 53:4](Isa.53.4) seems to indicate that Jesus’ power over sickness derives in some way from his death for sin, which was to be accomplished at the end of his ministry.

It is also interesting that Matthew, in relating Jesus’ healing of the multitudes by the sea ([Mt 12:15-21](Matt.12.15-Matt.12.21); cf. [Mk 3:7-12](Mark.3.7-Mark.3.12)), cites [Isaiah 42:1-4](Isa.42.1-Isa.42.4). This OT passage speaks of God’s servant anointed with the Spirit to proclaim justice to the nations. As used by Matthew, the quotation explains why Jesus commanded those healed not to make him known. Jesus did not want too much publicity about himself to thwart God’s plan for him as the Suffering Servant who was to bring salvation to the nations. This action demonstrates that Jesus’ healings are revelations of his person. Again another quotation from Isaiah ([6:9-10](Isa.6.9-Isa.6.10)) in [Matthew 13:14-15](Matt.13.14-Matt.13.15) brings out the fact that healing is understood primarily in the spiritual sense of hearing Jesus’ proclamation of the kingdom of God.

Luke, like Matthew and Mark, portrays Jesus preaching and healing. After the account of the birth of John and Jesus and the ministry of John the Baptist, Luke presents Jesus preaching in Nazareth ([Lk 4:16-30](Luke.4.16-Luke.4.30)). Here, in the synagogue of his hometown, Jesus himself, using a quotation from [Isaiah 61:1-2](Isa.61.1-Isa.61.2), affirms that the Spirit has anointed him to proclaim good news and to announce release for the captives and a recovery of sight for the blind ([Lk 4:18](Luke.4.18)). The healing aspect of Jesus’ ministry occupies an important place in the rest of the book of Luke. Indeed, Luke has all the healing incidents noted by Mark, except for those in [Mark 6:45–8:26](Mark.6.45-Mark.8.26). However, Luke’s opening scene in Nazareth seems to underscore that Jesus’ healing is to be understood, not as merely expressing Jesus’ compassion for the needy, but primarily as a sign of the arrival of the kingdom of God as promised in the Scriptures.

This emphasis may be seen in the distinctively Lukan account of the commissioning of the 72 disciples ([Lk 10:1-12](Luke.10.1-Luke.10.12)), where Jesus instructs them to heal the sick in any city they enter and announce to the people there that the kingdom of God has come near to them (vv [8-9](Luke.10.8-Luke.10.9)).

The first three Gospels take up the OT understanding of God as the healer of his people and see this as fulfilled in Jesus. This fulfillment signifies the presence of God’s reign in the ministry of Jesus and points to him as the one through whom God is at work in the midst of his people.

John’s Gospel has only four healing incidents: the official’s son ([Jn 4:46-54](John.4.46-John.4.54)), the man ill for 38 years ([5:1-18](John.5.1-John.5.18)), the man born blind (ch [9](John.9.1-John.9.41)), and the climactic raising of Lazarus ([11:1-44](John.11.1-John.11.44)). The special purpose and structure of this Gospel indicate that these incidents are carefully related to the accompanying discourses and are clearly intended as signs revealing the person of Jesus. The heightened emphasis on healings as revelatory signs in this Gospel confirms the similar intention in the first three Gospels.
Healings Done by the Apostles

The Acts of the Apostles tells of the continuation of Jesus’ ministry through the Spirit at work in his disciples. The primary focus in Acts is on proclamation, as [1:8](Acts.1.8) indicates. However, the healing of the lame beggar in Jerusalem indicates that the disciples were able to exercise the power of healing in the name of Jesus ([3:1-16](Acts.3.1-Acts.3.16); [4:8-16](Acts.4.8-Acts.4.16)). The healing is clearly intended to point to and glorify the person of Jesus and lead to faith in him ([3:12-26](Acts.3.12-Acts.3.26)). The balanced, twofold ministry of the disciples may be seen in the prayer of [4:29-30](Acts.4.29-Acts.4.30): “O Lord, hear their threats, and give your servants great boldness in their preaching. Send your healing power; may miraculous signs and wonders be done through the name of your holy servant Jesus” (NLT).

The ministry of Philip in Samaria was devoted to proclaiming Christ ([Acts 8:5](Acts.8.5)) and healing the sick and those with unclean spirits (v [7](Acts.8.7)). Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha ([9:34, 40](Acts.9.34 Acts.9.40)), and in each case the effects are that many believe in the Lord (vv [35, 42](Acts.9.35 Acts.9.42)). Paul is also described as preaching the gospel ([17:2-3](Acts.17.2-Acts.17.3)), healing ([14:8-11](Acts.14.8-Acts.14.11); [28:8](Acts.28.8)), casting out spirits ([16:18](Acts.16.18)), and raising a dead man ([20:9-10](Acts.20.9-Acts.20.10)).
Healings in the Church Age

The letters of the NT say little about healing. First Corinthians speaks of the gifts of healing ([1 Cor 12:9, 28](1Cor.12.9 1Cor.12.28)). The implication is that such gifts are intended to be part of the ministry of the church, but the context indicates that not all are given such gifts (v [30](1Cor.12.30)) and that it is God who sovereignly distributes gifts for the good of the body. James indicates that a believer who is ill should request the church to pray for his healing ([Jas 5:14-16](Jas.5.14-Jas.5.16); cf. [Heb 12:13](Heb.12.13)). The clear implication is that God is willing and able to minister to his people for healing today.
*See* [Spiritual Gifts](dictionary:SpiritualGifts).
Vital bodily organ; emotional center of one’s being.

In Hebrew and Greek, as in modern English, “heart” is used to designate a physical organ as well as the emotional center of one’s being. “Heart” (Hebrew *leb;* Greek *kardia*) occurs approximately 1,000 times in the Bible, though it is often disguised in translation. The range of meaning is great.
Physical Heart

That the beating heart indicates life seems implied in [1 Samuel 25:37-39](1Sam.25.37-1Sam.25.39) (see NLT mg), despite the delay in Nabal’s death. Physical food and wine affect the heart ([Jgs 19:5](Judg.19.5); [Ps 104:15](Ps.104.15); [Acts 14:17](Acts.14.17)), and the heart can “faint” and “tremble.” The heart’s position in the body yields an obvious metaphor for “the center” ([Mt 12:40](Matt.12.40)).
Pyschological Heart

The heart attends intellectually (e.g., [Jer 12:11](Jer.12.11)); it also perceives ([Jn 12:40](John.12.40)), understands ([1 Kgs 3:9](1Kgs.3.9)), debates ([Mk 2:6](Mark.2.6)), reflects ([Lk 2:19](Luke.2.19)), remembers ([Lk 2:51](Luke.2.51)), thinks ([Dt 8:17](Deut.8.17)), imagines ([Lk 1:51](Luke.1.51)), is wise ([Eccl 1:17](Eccl.1.17), KJV), has technical skill ([Ex 28:3](Exod.28.3), KJV), and much more.

Emotionally, the heart experiences intoxicated merriment ([1 Sm 25:36](1Sam.25.36)), gladness ([Is 30:29](Isa.30.29)), joy ([Jn 16:22](John.16.22)), sorrow ([Neh 2:2](Neh.2.2)), anguish ([Rom 9:2](Rom.9.2)), bitterness ([Prv 14:10](Prov.14.10)), anxiety ([1 Sm 4:13](1Sam.4.13)), despair ([Eccl 2:20](Eccl.2.20)), love ([2 Sm 14:1](2Sam.14.1)), trust ([Ps 112:7](Ps.112.7)), affection ([2 Cor 7:3](2Cor.7.3)), lust ([Mt 5:28](Matt.5.28)), callousness ([Mk 3:5](Mark.3.5)), hatred ([Lv 19:17](Lev.19.17)), fear ([Gn 42:28](Gen.42.28)), jealousy ([Jas 3:14](Jas.3.14)), desire ([Rom 10:1](Rom.10.1)), discouragement ([Nm 32:9](Num.32.9)), sympathy ([Ex 23:9](Exod.23.9)), anger ([Dt 19:6](Deut.19.6), KJV), irresolution ([2 Chr 13:7](2Chr.13.7), KJV), and much more.

Volitionally, the heart can purpose ([1 Cor 4:5](1Cor.4.5)), incline to ([1 Sm 14:7](1Sam.14.7)), prompt ([2 Kgs 12:4](2Kgs.12.4); cf. [Prv 4:23](Prov.4.23)), be steadfast ([Acts 11:23](Acts.11.23)), be willing ([Ex 35:22](Exod.35.22)), contrive evil ([Acts 5:4](Acts.5.4)), or follow its “treasure” ([Mt 6:21](Matt.6.21)).

Morally, the heart can be gentle, lowly ([Mt 11:29](Matt.11.29)), holy ([1 Thes 3:13](1Thess.3.13)), faithful ([Neh 9:8](Neh.9.8)), upright ([Ps 97:11](Ps.97.11)), pure, single-minded ([Jas 4:8](Jas.4.8)), clean ([Acts 15:8](Acts.15.8)), loving toward God ([Mk 12:30](Mark.12.30)) and others ([1 Pt 1:22](1Pet.1.22)), hardened, or sensitive ([Ez 11:19](Ezek.11.19)). Scripture’s emphasis falls upon the heart’s evil ([Gn 6:5](Gen.6.5) and throughout), as self-deceiving ([Jas 1:26](Jas.1.26)), deceitful ([Jer 17:9](Jer.17.9)), avaricious ([Mt 6:19-21](Matt.6.19-Matt.6.21)), lustful ([Mt 5:28](Matt.5.28)), arrogant ([Is 9:9](Isa.9.9)), impious ([Acts 7:51](Acts.7.51)), perverse ([Ps 101:4](Ps.101.4)), and impenitent ([Rom 2:5](Rom.2.5)). Nothing defiles a man worse than his own heart ([Mk 7:18-19](Mark.7.18-Mark.7.19)).

Yet out of the heart can come good ([Lk 6:45](Luke.6.45); [8:15](Luke.8.15)). Even when frustrated by circumstances or by fear, the heart’s good intention remains good; its evil intent, bad ([1 Kgs 8:18](1Kgs.8.18); [Mt 5:28](Matt.5.28)).

Being so complex, a person’s heart is sadly divided, and Scripture often extols a perfect, whole, true (i.e., united) heart ([Gn 20:5](Gen.20.5); [Ps 86:11](Ps.86.11); [Acts 8:37](Acts.8.37)). The “heart” signifies the total inner self, a person’s hidden core of being ([1 Pt 3:4](1Pet.3.4)), with which one communes, which one “pours out” in prayer, words, and deeds ([Ps 62:8](Ps.62.8); [Mt 15:18-19](Matt.15.18-Matt.15.19)). It is the genuine self, distinguished from appearance, public position, and physical presence ([1 Sm 16:7](1Sam.16.7); [2 Cor 5:12](2Cor.5.12); [1 Thes 2:17](1Thess.2.17)). And this “heart-self” has its own nature, character, and disposition ([Dn 4:16](Dan.4.16); [7:4](Dan.7.4), KJV; cf. [Mt 12:33-37](Matt.12.33-Matt.12.37)).
The Spiritual Heart

The heart is especially important in biblical religion. The mystery of the hidden self is fully known to God and to Christ ([Jer 17:10](Jer.17.10); [Lk 9:47](Luke.9.47); [Rom 8:27](Rom.8.27)), and the heart is the seat of our knowledge of God ([2 Cor 4:6](2Cor.4.6)). The state of heart governs the vision of God ([Mt 5:8](Matt.5.8)); from the heart one speaks to God ([Ps 27:8](Ps.27.8)); the heart is the locus of divine indwelling ([2 Cor 1:22](2Cor.1.22); [Gal 4:6](Gal.4.6); [Eph 3:17](Eph.3.17)).

On the other hand, moral evil in the heart is seen in biblical perspective as sin against God. Senseless hearts are darkened, often secretly idolatrous, far from God, “not right” before God ([Dt 29:18-19](Deut.29.18-Deut.29.19); [Mt 15:8](Matt.15.8); [Acts 8:21](Acts.8.21); [Rom 1:21](Rom.1.21)). Yet the Lord will not despise a broken, contrite heart ([Ps 51:17](Ps.51.17)). When one’s heart is turned toward God, he promises to make it sensitive to divine things, renewed and purified ([Dt 4:29](Deut.4.29); [2 Kgs 23:25](2Kgs.23.25); [Ps 51:10](Ps.51.10); [Jl 2:13](Joel.2.13); [Ez 36:25-27](Ezek.36.25-Ezek.36.27)). God’s law shall then be written on the heart as the inward guide and incentive ([Jer 31:33](Jer.31.33); [Heb 8:10](Heb.8.10); cf. [2 Cor 3:2-3](2Cor.3.2-2Cor.3.3)).

In Christian terms, such transformation involves believing the gospel from the “honest and good heart” that provides fruitful soil for the Word of God ([Lk 8:15](Luke.8.15); [Rom 10:9](Rom.10.9)). The true heart draws near to God, loves him with all its intellect, feeling, and will ([Lk 10:27](Luke.10.27); [Heb 10:22](Heb.10.22)). Then God gives strength, reward, renewal, grace, peace, and joy to the heart ([Ps 73:26](Ps.73.26); [Is 57:15](Isa.57.15); [Acts 2:46](Acts.2.46); [Phil 4:7](Phil.4.7); [Heb 13:9](Heb.13.9)). So the ancient ideal becomes possible again, that of being “a man after God’s own heart” ([1 Sm 13:14](1Sam.13.14); [Acts 13:22](Acts.13.22)).
*See* [Homes and Dwellings](dictionary:HomesandDwellings).
Type of evergreen shrub; KJV mistranslation for shrub or bush in [Jeremiah 17:6](Jer.17.6) and [48:6](Jer.48.6). *See* [Plants (Juniper)](dictionary:Plants).

Realm (or realms) designated by a Hebrew term used to represent the sky and air and also heaven. The form of the word in Hebrew is dual (implying two of something). Although this dual form may only represent an ancient device for expressing the plural, it is supposed by some to imply the existence of a lower and an upper heaven—a physical and a spiritual heaven.
In the Old Testament

The OT writers viewed the physical heavens as a “firmament” appearing as a great arch supported on foundations and pillars ([2 Sm 22:8](2Sam.22.8)) and spread out above the earth, with rain descending through its doors ([Ps 78:23](Ps.78.23)). The keynote of the OT revelation about the physical heavens is set forth in [Psalms 8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9) and [19:1-6](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.6). Elsewhere the OT speaks of the atmospheric heavens as the region of the clouds ([Ps 147:8](Ps.147.8)), winds ([Zec 2:6](Zech.2.6)), rain ([Dt 11:11](Deut.11.11)), thunder ([1 Sm 2:10](1Sam.2.10)), dew ([Dt 33:13](Deut.33.13)), frost ([Jb 38:29](Job.38.29)), and the abode of birds ([Gn 1:26, 30](Gen.1.26 Gen.1.30)). It is also the locale of such destructive forces as hail ([Jos 10:11](Josh.10.11)), fire, and brimstone ([Gn 19:24](Gen.19.24)). In the NT this notion of the vaulted expanse of the sky as the region in which the elements, clouds, and tempests gather ([Mt 16:2](Matt.16.2); [Lk 4:25](Luke.4.25)) and birds fly ([Lk 9:58](Luke.9.58)) is continued.

In addition to the atmospheric regions, the Hebrew idea of the physical heavens includes stellar space, which ultimately embraces the universe. The heavenly bodies of the stellar heavens were viewed by the Hebrews as inexpressibly glorious manifestations of God’s handiwork without having any power or vitality of their own. These include the sun, moon, planets, and stars, which were but lights in the firmament of the heavens ([Gn 1:14](Gen.1.14); [15:5](Gen.15.5)). As such, they were regarded as unworthy of worship because God had, by his own will and grace, made humans superior to them. In fact, the Hebrews were expressly forbidden to worship the stellar bodies ([Ex 20:4](Exod.20.4)), the gods and goddesses who represented them ([Jer 44:17-25](Jer.44.17-Jer.44.25)), or to participate in astrological speculation ([Is 47:13](Isa.47.13)). Hence, this unique theological ordinance differentiated the Hebrews, who viewed the heavenly bodies as made and moved by the will of God, from the superstitious heathen, who worshiped them.

The term “heaven of heavens” ([Dt 10:14](Deut.10.14); see also KJV [1 Kgs 8:27](1Kgs.8.27); [Pss 68:33](Ps.68.33); [148:4](Ps.148.4)) is the literal English rendition of the Hebrew idiom for the superlative “the highest heaven.” Some have thought this the counterpart to Paul’s expression “the third heaven” ([2 Cor 12:2](2Cor.12.2)), which parallels the classical Greek conception of three heavens.
